result.headline: The spec's entire "passive sensing" premise is an OS-vendor privilege, not an app capability: Google's PHRM works because Google owns the face-unlock path on Pixel, and BOTH iOS and Android hard-block third-party background/on-unlock camera and unlock-event detection. Every passive-capture feature must be rewritten as a foreground, user-initiated 30-second measurement — and the wearable/CGM sync chapter must be deleted outright under the no-external-devices constraint.

findings.claimOrFeature: Passive front-camera rPPG capture on iOS while the app is backgrounded or immediately on unlock (PHRM-style)
findings.reality: iOS has no camera background mode. The moment the app leaves the foreground, AVCaptureSession is interrupted with AVCaptureSession.InterruptionReason.videoDeviceNotAvailableInBackground — the docs state this reason 'indicates that the video device is not available because the app is running in the background.' The session is preserved but produces no frames until the app returns to the foreground. Separately, since iOS 14 a green indicator is shown whenever the camera is in use, on the Home Screen and in other apps, and an app cannot suppress it in code. There is also no mechanism to launch or resume the app on unlock, so 'capture on unlock' has no trigger even in principle.
findings.evidence: Apple: 'AVCaptureSession.InterruptionReason.videoDeviceNotAvailableInBackground — the video device is not available because the app is running in the background.' Apple Privacy: 'when an app uses the microphone or camera, your device displays an indicator... whether you are in the app, in another app, or on the Home Screen.'
findings.correction: Delete 'passive/background heart-rate capture' from the iOS spec. Replace with an explicit, foreground, user-initiated measurement: user opens the app, taps 'Take a reading', holds still for 20-30s with the front camera (or finger-over-rear-camera + torch PPG, which is far more robust). Frequency becomes 1-3 user-initiated readings/day, not continuous. Every downstream metric (resting HR trend, HRV trend) must be re-scoped to sparse, self-selected samples.

findings.claimOrFeature: Passive front-camera capture on Android from a background service or on ACTION_USER_PRESENT
findings.reality: Android 9 (API 28) blocked camera access for apps running in the background. The only escape hatch is a foreground service of type 'camera' — but CAMERA is a while-in-use permission, so a camera FGS cannot be started while the app is in the background at all. On Android 14+ the system throws SecurityException at service creation. So the capture can only ever begin from a visible activity, which means the user is already looking at the app — i.e. it is not passive.
findings.evidence: Android: 'The CAMERA runtime permission is subject to while-in-use restrictions. For this reason, you cannot create a camera foreground service while your app is in the background and you cannot launch a camera foreground service from a BOOT_COMPLETED receiver.' And: 'If your app is in the background and it creates a foreground service of type camera, location, or microphone, the system sees that your app doesn't currently have the required permissions, and it throws a SecurityException.'
findings.correction: Same as iOS: foreground, user-initiated measurement only. Do not spec a 'camera foreground service' as the Android workaround — it does not unlock passive capture, it only lets an already-foregrounded session survive backgrounding, which is not the use case.

findings.claimOrFeature: 'Inspired by Google's PHRM' — implying a small team can replicate passive heart-rate monitoring during everyday phone use
findings.reality: PHRM is not a third-party app capability and was never shipped as one. Google's own description is that the system captures a short (~8s) facial video after the user unlocks the phone with face authentication, and runs an on-device model. The trigger is the OS face-unlock event — a hook available only to the platform owner. It is also published as research (Nature / arXiv, 192k training videos, 485 participants), not as a public API or SDK. Citing it as precedent for what your app will do is the single most dangerous line in the spec: it will read to a judge or investor as 'this is proven, we just implement it.'
findings.evidence: Google Research: PHRM 'captures short facial videos after a user unlocks their phone [with face authentication]' and runs an on-device model; described as 'the first large-scale demonstration of passive HR and daily RHR monitoring during everyday smartphone use' — a research result, with no third-party API.
findings.correction: Rewrite the citation as: 'Google Research has shown (Nature, 2026) that smartphone-camera rPPG can estimate heart rate at <10% MAPE — but only via an OS-level hook into face unlock that is unavailable to third-party apps. We therefore use the same underlying signal (camera PPG) in an active, user-initiated 30-second measurement.' Never let 'PHRM-inspired' stand next to the word 'passive' in the same feature.

findings.claimOrFeature: Detect device unlock on iOS to trigger a measurement or infer sleep/wake and phone-use patterns
findings.reality: There is no public iOS API for lock/unlock events, and no mechanism to wake the app on unlock. Apple DTS has answered this directly. UIApplication.isProtectedDataAvailable / protectedDataDidBecomeAvailableNotification is the only adjacent signal, and it only fires for a process that is already running — it is a file-protection signal, not an unlock counter. The private SpringBoard notifications (com.apple.springboard.lockstate / lockcomplete) are a documented App Store rejection cause. The Screen Time stack (FamilyControls / DeviceActivity) is not a substitute: it requires the com.apple.developer.family-controls entitlement, which Apple grants case-by-case and is scoped to parental-control/screen-wellbeing use, and it reports app-usage thresholds, not raw unlock events.
findings.evidence: Apple DTS Engineer: 'I don't see any way to do that programmatically... For this to work the system would have to resume (or relaunch) your app in the background every time the device is unlocked, and there's no facility to do that.' Plus: 'The only other way... would be for the system to maintain these metrics for you, and give you access to them via some API. Again, there's no API for that.'
findings.correction: Remove unlock-count / unlock-triggered capture from the iOS spec entirely. Substitute signals that ARE available without user action: CMPedometer / HKQuantityTypeIdentifier.stepCount (phone-only, no wearable), which supports historical queries and gives a defensible activity + sedentary-time proxy; and app-open timestamps for the app's own engagement rhythm. Be honest in the spec that iOS gives zero device-usage telemetry to third parties.

findings.claimOrFeature: Detect device unlock on Android via ACTION_USER_PRESENT / ACTION_SCREEN_ON
findings.reality: Technically reachable but expensive and fragile. Neither ACTION_USER_PRESENT nor ACTION_SCREEN_ON/SCREEN_OFF appears on Android's implicit-broadcast exemption list, so a manifest-declared receiver will not fire for apps targeting API 26+ (mandatory on Play). The only route is Context.registerReceiver() at runtime from a live process — which means keeping a foreground service alive 24/7 with a permanent notification, an FGS type you must justify in Play Console, plus battery drain and India-specific OEM aggressive-kill behaviour (Xiaomi/MIUI, Oppo/ColorOS, Vivo, Realme, Samsung) that silently terminates such services. And even when it fires, ACTION_USER_PRESENT gives you a timestamp, not permission to open the camera — see the camera finding.
findings.evidence: Android's 'Implicit broadcast exceptions' list enumerates every broadcast still deliverable to manifest receivers (BOOT_COMPLETED, TIME_SET, LOCALE_CHANGED, USB, Bluetooth, telephony, SMS, media, etc.). ACTION_USER_PRESENT, ACTION_SCREEN_ON and ACTION_SCREEN_OFF are absent from it.
findings.correction: Do not put unlock-event tracking on the critical path, and never spec it as cross-platform (it can never work on iOS, so any feature built on it is Android-only by construction). If retained, spec it as an opt-in Android-only 'phone rhythm' beta with an always-on notification, an explicit battery-cost disclosure, and a per-OEM autostart whitelist onboarding flow. Budget engineering time for OEM kill-behaviour QA — this is a multi-week tax on a 4-person team.

findings.claimOrFeature: Overnight background microphone recording on iOS for snore / sleep-sound detection
findings.reality: Possible but only under conditions the spec must state. Recording cannot be *started* in the background — the session must begin while the app is in the foreground, after which Apple allows it to continue indefinitely in the background, surfaced to the user as the persistent orange indicator. Review risk is real: guideline 2.5.4 restricts background modes to their intended purposes and Apple has rejected apps using the 'audio' mode for non-audible-content purposes; 2.5.14 additionally requires explicit consent and a clear visual/audible indication of recording. Practically, the shipping category confirms the constraint: SnoreLab instructs users to leave the app running and the phone unlocked, using the proximity sensor to blank the screen rather than truly backgrounding.
findings.evidence: Apple DTS: 'we allow apps that start an audio recording session in the foreground to continue recording indefinitely in the background. That's visible to the user as the orange pill in the status bar.' Guideline 2.5.14: 'Apps must request explicit user consent and provide a clear visual and/or audible indication when recording, logging, or otherwise making a record of user activity.'
findings.correction: Spec it as: user must open the app and tap 'Start night' before sleeping; phone must be on charge; orange recording indicator visible all night; audio analysed on-device and discarded (never uploaded) — say this explicitly in the spec, because uploading overnight bedroom audio is a review and trust catastrophe. Add a review-risk line item: prepare a 2.5.4/2.5.14 justification for App Review before the first submission.

findings.claimOrFeature: Overnight background microphone on Android via a persistent service
findings.reality: Requires RECORD_AUDIO plus FOREGROUND_SERVICE_MICROPHONE and android:foregroundServiceType="microphone", and — like camera — RECORD_AUDIO is while-in-use, so the service must be started from a visible activity. It cannot self-start at bedtime, cannot start from BOOT_COMPLETED, and shows a permanent notification. The India-first target makes this materially worse: aggressive OEM battery managers routinely kill long-running foreground services overnight, producing silent data loss users will read as 'the app is broken'.
findings.evidence: Android: 'The RECORD_AUDIO runtime permission is subject to while-in-use restrictions. For this reason, you cannot create a microphone foreground service while your app is in the background and you cannot launch a microphone foreground service from a BOOT_COMPLETED receiver.'
findings.correction: Spec an explicit user-initiated 'Start night' action (same as iOS — keeps the two platforms behaviourally identical), an onboarding step that walks the user through disabling battery optimisation for the app, and graceful handling of truncated nights. Also declare the microphone FGS type and its justification in Play Console; expect scrutiny.

findings.claimOrFeature: Typing speed / keystroke dynamics captured OUTSIDE the app as a 'brain fog' proxy
findings.reality: On iOS this is flatly impossible: there is no API exposing keystrokes in other apps. The only system-wide text path is a custom keyboard extension, which requires the user to install it, switch to it, and grant 'Full Access' — and harvesting keystroke timing through it for health inference is precisely the pattern App Review treats as covert user-activity logging under 2.5.14. On Android the only route is AccessibilityService, and Play policy restricts the accessibility-tool designation to services that genuinely help users with disabilities; any other use requires a Play Console declaration form, in-app prominent disclosure, affirmative consent and video evidence of the flow. 'Brain fog measurement' is not an accessibility purpose, and Google states non-declared or deceptive use can suspend the app and terminate the developer account. For a 4-person team this is an account-level bet on a secondary proxy metric.
findings.evidence: Google Play: 'Deceptive and non-declared uses of these APIs may result in a suspension of your app and/or termination of your developer account'; only services 'designed to help people with disabilities' may declare themselves accessibility tools, all other uses require a declaration, prominent in-app disclosure, affirmative consent and video evidence.
findings.correction: Move the entire keystroke-dynamics feature INSIDE the app. The app already has a symptom journal / check-in text field: instrument that. Inter-key interval, backspace rate, and time-to-first-keystroke inside your own UITextView/EditText need zero special permission, are cross-platform, and are defensible in a privacy policy. Add a foreground reaction-time / n-back mini-game (10-20s) as the primary cognitive measure — that is the shippable version of 'brain fog'.

findings.claimOrFeature: Apple HealthKit as a data source for HR, sleep and activity
findings.reality: HealthKit is shippable, but two constraints break the spec's assumptions. (1) It is native-iOS only: there is no HealthKit REST/web API, no OAuth flow, and no way to pull a user's data from your backend — data is on-device and only your iOS app can read and forward it. (2) Under the no-external-devices rule, HealthKit on an iPhone-with-no-Watch contains essentially only what the phone itself produces — step count, distance, flights climbed from the motion coprocessor — plus whatever the user typed in manually. There is no phone-only heart rate, HRV, SpO2, or automatic sleep staging in HealthKit. Reading 'sleep/HR from HealthKit' therefore silently reintroduces the wearable requirement. Guideline 5.1.3 also bars using HealthKit-derived data for advertising or use-based data mining and requires disclosing exactly which health data you collect.
findings.evidence: Apple guideline 5.1.3(i): apps 'may not use or disclose to third parties data gathered in the health, fitness, and medical research context—including from the Clinical Health Records API, HealthKit API, Motion and Fitness... for advertising, marketing, or other use-based data mining purposes'; 'You must disclose the specific health data that you are collecting from the device.' HealthKit exposes no server-side API — all reads are through the on-device native app.
findings.correction: In the spec, split HealthKit reads into (a) phone-native, always-available: stepCount, distanceWalkingRunning, flightsClimbed, appleSleepingWristTemperature=NO, sleepAnalysis only if user-logged; and (b) wearable-dependent: HR, HRV, SpO2, automatic sleep stages — explicitly labelled 'only present if the user already owns a Watch; never assumed.' Delete any architecture diagram showing a server pulling from HealthKit.

findings.claimOrFeature: Google Fit APIs for reading steps / sleep / HR on Android
findings.reality: Google Fit is dead for new builds. Developers have not been able to sign up for the Fit APIs since May 1, 2024, and the APIs (including the Fit REST API) are supported only until the end of 2026 — i.e. they expire inside this product's first year. The REST API has no successor at all, which kills any server-side Android health-data pull. The replacement, Health Connect, is Android-only and on-device, so it gives no cross-platform parity with HealthKit and no cloud path. Health Connect access also requires a Play Console health-apps declaration with per-data-type justification, and reading data while backgrounded or reading history needs additional separately-declared permissions.
findings.evidence: Google Fit Migration FAQ: 'Developers cannot sign up to use these APIs as of May 1, 2024'; 'Google Fit APIs will be supported until the end of 2026'; and on the REST API: 'There is no alternative to the Fit REST API.' Health Connect: 'To read data while your app is in the background, or to read historical data, an additional set of read permissions must be declared separately.'
findings.correction: Strike every mention of Google Fit from the spec and replace with Health Connect (androidx.health.connect). Add the Play Console health-apps declaration and the READ_HEALTH_DATA_IN_BACKGROUND / history permissions as explicit pre-launch tasks with per-data-type justification text. Note in the architecture section that all health-data reads are on-device on BOTH platforms — there is no cloud sync path on either.

findings.claimOrFeature: Wearable and CGM sync (smartwatch HR/HRV/sleep stages, continuous glucose, BP cuff) as spec features
findings.reality: This entire chapter violates the stated hard constraint. CGM in particular is not merely a hardware purchase — in India, CGM sensors are consumable, prescription-adjacent, and cost ~₹4,000-6,000 per 14 days, so any feature keyed to them excludes the overwhelming majority of the target user base. The softer 'import from a device the user already owns' framing is a genuine grey zone but not a rescue: on iOS it lands in HealthKit and on Android in Health Connect, two non-interoperable, on-device-only stores, so a feature built on it has different data availability per platform and is absent for the median user who owns no wearable at all.
findings.evidence: Health Connect is documented as an Android-only, on-device data layer; HealthKit has no web/server API and is native-iOS only — so there is no single cross-platform path for imported device data, and no device-independent path for HR/HRV/glucose at all.
findings.correction: Remove wearable and CGM sync from the core spec and the roadmap's first two phases. If retained at all, put it in an explicitly-labelled 'Optional enrichment (v2, grey zone)' appendix with the sentence: 'No feature, score, or insight may degrade or become unavailable if the user has no connected device.' Make that a testable acceptance criterion, not a principle. Any phone-only glucose or BP inference from camera/audio is separately not shippable and should not appear anywhere in the document.

findings.claimOrFeature: Ship the product as a PWA (India-first, avoid app stores)
findings.reality: A PWA cannot deliver this product's sensing core. There is no web API for HealthKit or Health Connect — both are native-only. getUserMedia camera/mic capture requires a visible, foregrounded page and stops when the page is backgrounded, so neither overnight audio nor any passive capture works. The Background Synchronization API is explicitly 'not Baseline because it does not work in some of the most widely-used browsers' and is unsupported in Safari, so reliable background upload/sync on iOS does not exist. Web Push on iOS works only for web apps the user has manually added to the Home Screen (16.4+), with no install prompt and no push at all from a Safari tab — a severe funnel loss for a habit product that depends on daily reminders. iOS also evicts PWA storage after periods of non-use, which can silently destroy locally-stored longitudinal health data.
findings.evidence: MDN on Background Synchronization API: 'Limited availability — This feature is not Baseline because it does not work in some of the most widely-used browsers.' WebKit: Web Push is available to 'a web app that has been added to the Home Screen', requiring direct user interaction to request permission, from iOS/iPadOS 16.4.
findings.correction: Spec native (or React Native / Flutter) as the only delivery vehicle for anything touching camera, microphone, motion or health stores. If a PWA is wanted for India reach, scope it explicitly to the non-sensing surface — cycle logging, symptom journal, education content, dashboard viewing — and state that camera measurement, overnight audio, and HealthKit/Health Connect import are native-only. Do not let a single roadmap item assume feature parity between the PWA and the app.

findings.claimOrFeature: iOS Screen Time / DeviceActivity as a workaround for unlock and phone-usage sensing
findings.reality: Not a viable substitute. The FamilyControls / DeviceActivity / ManagedSettings stack requires the com.apple.developer.family-controls entitlement, which must be individually requested from Apple with a justification and is granted case-by-case for parental-control and screen-wellbeing products; it must be requested for every app target that uses it. Third-party apps receive only a restricted subset of what Apple's own Screen Time app can do. What it surfaces is app-usage thresholds and shielding controls — not raw unlock events, not per-unlock timestamps, and not anything usable to trigger a camera capture (which is blocked regardless).
findings.evidence: Apple's 'Requesting the Family Controls entitlement' documentation requires an explicit application with justification through the developer portal; third-party apps 'only receive a carefully controlled subset of the capabilities available to Apple's own system app.'
findings.correction: Do not list Screen Time APIs as a mitigation for the unlock-detection block. If the spec wants a phone-usage signal, source it from in-app engagement telemetry only (session starts, session length, time-of-day of check-ins) and label it honestly as engagement data rather than device-usage data.

result.headline: Exactly two camera signals are genuinely shippable and validated — fingertip contact PPG heart rate (rear camera + torch, MAPE 1.6%) and front-camera respiratory rate (MAE 0.78 br/min) — and both are 30-second ACTIVE spot checks, never passive: neither iOS nor Android lets a third-party app open the camera in the background. Everything else in the sensing stack is either scientifically contested (facial-AU stress, voice mood), research-only (overnight BCG, hirsutism scoring), or explicitly banned from the App Store by Guideline 1.4.1, which names blood pressure, blood oxygen, blood glucose and body temperature "using only the sensors on the device" as not permitted — killing camera SpO2 and PTT blood pressure outright on iOS.

findings.claimOrFeature: Contact PPG heart rate — fingertip on rear camera with flash/torch
findings.reality: This is the one camera vital sign with a large prospective validation behind it. Google's study of 95 participants (rest + post-exercise) using finger-over-rear-camera reported mean absolute percent error of 1.6% ± 4.3% against reference, beating a pre-specified 5% goal, with no significant difference across colorimeter-measured skin tone groups (1.8% very light–intermediate, 1.3% tan/brown, 1.8% dark). A small team can rebuild this: it is classical DSP, not deep learning. Failure modes are pressing too hard (occludes capillary bed, flattens waveform), finger movement, cold fingers/vasoconstriction, and torch heat on long captures.
findings.evidence: "In the HR study of 95 participants... the mean absolute percent error (MAPE) was 1.6% ± 4.3%, which was significantly lower than the pre-specified goal of 5%. No significant differences in the MAPE were present across colorimeter-measured skin-tone subgroups." Study devices were Pixel 3 and Pixel 4.
findings.correction: Make this the flagship demo and the ONLY heart-rate claim in v1. Build spec: rear camera, torch ON continuously, lock AE/AWB/focus (auto-exposure hunting is the #1 signal killer), capture 30s at 30 fps minimum (60 fps if the device offers it), ROI = full frame mean of the RED channel (saturated red under torch; green is the right channel for face rPPG but red for fingertip transmission). Chain: per-frame spatial mean → detrend (smoothness-priors, λ≈10) → 4th-order Butterworth bandpass 0.7–3.5 Hz (42–210 bpm) → normalize → Welch PSD/FFT with zero-padding for the dominant peak, cross-checked against adaptive-threshold peak detection; reject the reading if peak-to-second-peak ratio is low or if >20% of frames fail a red-saturation/finger-present check. Show a live waveform — that is the showpiece. Quote ±3 bpm, not a decimal. Implement natively (AVFoundation / CameraX ImageAnalysis) — a PWA cannot reliably control the torch plus locked exposure.

findings.claimOrFeature: Passive/ambient camera sensing — the app measures heart rate "in the background" while the user does other things
findings.reality: No third-party app on iOS or Android can open the camera while backgrounded. On Android, a foreground service started while the app is in the background cannot access the camera or microphone at all, and there is no camera equivalent of ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION; camera access is strictly while-in-use. iOS suspends AVCaptureSession on backgrounding and has no background camera mode. Every camera-derived signal in this spec is therefore an ACTIVE, user-initiated, screen-on spot measurement.
findings.evidence: "If an app starts a foreground service while running in the background, the foreground service cannot access the microphone or camera" (Android 11/12+); apps targeting Android 12+ generally cannot start a foreground service from the background at all. Camera and microphone foreground service types must be declared and are while-in-use only.
findings.correction: Delete the word "passive" from every camera feature in the spec and rewrite as "30-second guided check-in." Reserve "passive" strictly for signals that genuinely run in background: accelerometer/pedometer step and activity data (HealthKit/Health Connect reads), screen-state and notification-interaction timing, and coarse sleep-window inference. Design the daily loop around one deliberate 60-second morning ritual (finger HR + breathing check) rather than an ambient always-on fiction — the ritual is also better retention design.

findings.claimOrFeature: Feature inspired by / positioned as equivalent to "Google PHRM passive heart rate monitoring"
findings.reality: Google's shipped, clinically validated smartphone heart rate feature is explicitly a CONTACT measurement — the user places a finger on the rear camera lens — and it is user-initiated, not passive. Only respiratory rate uses the front camera contactlessly. Citing Google as precedent for passive or contactless face-based heart rate misrepresents the source. Google also ships it as a Pixel-first feature with a full research org behind it, and Google Fit's developer APIs were sunset (support ended 30 June 2025) in favour of Health Connect — so "Google does it" is not a durable availability argument either.
findings.evidence: Google's own launch post: heart rate — "simply place your finger on the rear-facing camera lens"; respiratory rate — "place your head and upper torso in view of your phone's front-facing camera and breathe normally." Google adds: "These measurements aren't meant for medical diagnosis or to evaluate medical conditions."
findings.correction: Rewrite the precedent paragraph to: "Google Fit shipped camera-based heart rate as a user-initiated fingertip contact measurement and respiratory rate as a user-initiated front-camera measurement, both validated in Communications Medicine (2022) and both labelled non-diagnostic wellness features. We follow the same pattern and the same non-diagnostic framing." Do not use the phrase "passive heart rate monitoring" anywhere in investor or judge-facing material.

findings.claimOrFeature: Contactless face rPPG heart rate from the front camera
findings.reality: Real under controlled conditions, unreliable as a primary metric in the field. Best recent hybrid algorithms reach RMSE ≈ 2.0 bpm with r²=0.96 against time-aligned ECG — but that is a seated, well-lit, motion-controlled benchmark. Systematic evaluation of eight rPPG algorithms across three datasets found many methods degrade badly under low illumination and at elevated heart rates, which are precisely the two conditions a well-being app hits (evening use, post-stress). Additional field killers: warm/flickering Indian indoor lighting (LED PWM flicker beats in-band with the pulse), rolling-shutter artefacts, camera AE/AWB auto-adjusting mid-capture, makeup and foundation, and darker skin tones reducing the already-tiny green-channel modulation depth (~1% of pixel intensity). Classical methods (CHROM, POS) are buildable by a small team; the deep models that win benchmarks need training data you do not have.
findings.evidence: "Recent hybrid algorithms achieved RMSE as low as 2.0 bpm with an r² of 0.96 when evaluated against time-aligned electrocardiogram"; separately, npj Digital Medicine (2025) assessed eight rPPG algorithms across three datasets and found "many existing rPPG methods struggle under challenging conditions" of low illumination and elevated heart rates.
findings.correction: Ship face rPPG as a secondary, clearly-labelled "beta / experimental" reading, never as the number a symptom log correlates against. Build spec: front camera, flash OFF, 30 fps locked, exposure and white balance LOCKED before capture starts, 45–60 s capture, ROI = forehead + both cheeks via MediaPipe Face Mesh landmarks (skip lips, eyes, nostrils), per-ROI spatial mean of R/G/B → POS or CHROM chrominance combination (both are ~20 lines of NumPy and are in the public literature) → detrend → bandpass 0.7–3.5 Hz → Welch PSD peak. Gate the result on a live quality check (face-box motion variance, mean luminance ≥ ~150 lux equivalent, SNR of the spectral peak) and REFUSE to display a number when quality fails — a refusal is far better product than a wrong bpm. Prototype offline with rPPG-Toolbox (github.com/ubicomplab/rPPG-Toolbox) or pyVHR to pick the algorithm, then port POS/CHROM by hand to Swift/Kotlin. Quote ±5 bpm in good light.

findings.claimOrFeature: HRV (rMSSD) from smartphone PPG, used for biofeedback and for correlating with PMOS symptoms
findings.reality: Phone-PPG HRV is trustworthy for within-person trends under a fixed protocol, and not trustworthy for absolute values or fine-grained symptom correlation. The core problem is temporal resolution: a 30 fps camera gives 33 ms quantisation on inter-beat intervals, and rMSSD is the HRV metric most sensitive to that. Published work finds a minimum sampling rate of 50 Hz is needed for accurate RMSSD/SDNN without interpolation, though cubic-spline or parabolic interpolation of the PPG peaks brings relative absolute error back under 5%. Validation studies are mixed: some find good ECG agreement for NN, SDNN and RMSSD but insufficient agreement for LF/HF; others find RMSSD and pNN50 fail to reach acceptable agreement. A recent athlete study put phone-app RMSSD MAPE at 17.49% with wide limits of agreement. Respiration rate and posture confound HRV more than PMOS status will.
findings.evidence: "For normal variability signals without interpolation, the sampling rate must be at least 50 Hz for accurate RMSSD or SDNN"; "both cubic spline and parabola interpolation enhance the accuracy... with relative absolute error within 5% even at lower sampling rates." Athlete validation: "the PPG app demonstrat[ed] strong validity (RMSSD MAPE: 17.49%) but wider limits of agreement."
findings.correction: Ship HRV only as a personal-baseline z-score, never as an absolute rMSSD number the user can compare to a friend or to a Whoop. Build spec: fingertip contact PPG (rear camera + torch) — do NOT attempt HRV from face rPPG, the SNR is not there. Capture at the highest frame rate the device exposes (request 60/120 fps via AVCaptureDevice.activeVideoMinFrameDuration or CameraX/Camera2 AE target FPS range; fall back to 30 fps). Detect systolic peaks, then refine each peak location by parabolic or cubic-spline interpolation on the surrounding samples before computing IBIs — this step is mandatory, not optional. Duration: 3 minutes seated, same time each morning, before caffeine, with a fixed 6-breaths-per-minute paced-breathing prompt so respiration is held constant. Discard any recording with >5% ectopic/artefact beats. Require 14 days of baseline before showing any trend, and label the output "Recovery Score (relative to your own 14-day baseline)" rather than "HRV: 42 ms." For a paced-breathing biofeedback loop this is genuinely good enough and is a strong demo — the loop only needs relative change, not absolute accuracy.

findings.claimOrFeature: SpO2 / blood oxygen estimation from the phone camera
findings.reality: Blocked on three independent axes. (1) Policy: App Store Review Guideline 1.4.1 names this explicitly as not permitted. (2) Physics: clinical pulse oximetry needs 660 nm red and 940 nm IR because that is where HbO2 and Hb absorption diverge; phone RGB sensors have IR-cut filters and "very low quantum efficiency at infrared wavelengths," and the HbO2/Hb difference at green is too small to be usable. Red/green ratio workarounds exist but report ~2.9% RMS error, which is at or worse than the ±2–3% Arms bar for a regulated oximeter — and that is in-lab. (3) Market evidence: Samsung shipped a dedicated optical SpO2 sensor on phones from Note 4 through S10 and then removed it entirely; Apple had Blood Oxygen disabled on US Apple Watches from Jan 2024 under the Masimo ITC exclusion order, restoring it in Aug 2025 only by shifting the calculation to the iPhone. If Samsung with real hardware quit and Apple got sued, a four-person team with an RGB camera will not win this.
findings.evidence: Apple, Guideline 1.4.1: "apps that claim to take x-rays, measure blood pressure, body temperature, blood glucose levels, or blood oxygen levels using only the sensors on the device are not permitted." Physics: "The use of standard red and infrared LEDs for illumination on a consumer smartphone is not possible without modification of the smartphone hardware... the RGB sensors in the smartphone present very low quantum efficiency at infrared wavelengths."
findings.correction: Cut SpO2 from the spec entirely — not "phase 2," not "experimental," cut. There is no compliant path and no viable substitute on a phone. If the spec's underlying goal was fatigue or breathlessness tracking, replace it with the validated front-camera respiratory rate measurement plus a 2-item self-report. If the underlying goal was a sleep-apnoea signal (relevant in PMOS), replace with the STOP-BANG questionnaire delivered in-app as an educational screen with a referral prompt — non-diagnostic, zero sensing risk, and clinically more defensible than a camera number.

findings.claimOrFeature: Contactless respiratory rate from the front camera
findings.reality: The strongest contactless claim in the spec and the second validated Google feature. In a 50-participant prospective study, front-camera respiratory rate achieved mean absolute error of 0.78 ± 0.61 breaths/min against reference, against a pre-specified goal of 3 breaths/min. It works because it tracks gross chest/shoulder pixel motion at 0.1–0.7 Hz rather than subtle colour changes, so it is far more robust to skin tone and lighting than rPPG. Failure modes are real but bounded: the user must sit still (fidgeting swamps the breathing signal), the torso must be in frame, loose or high-contrast-patterned clothing helps while dark loose clothing hurts, and background motion (a family member walking past — common in Indian home settings) corrupts it.
findings.evidence: "In the RR study of 50 participants, the mean absolute error (MAE) was 0.78 ± 0.61 breaths/min, which was significantly lower than the pre-specified goal of 3 breaths/min." Measured by "a video of the participants sitting still in front of the front-facing camera."
findings.correction: Ship this as the second showpiece, paired with paced breathing. Build spec: front camera, flash off, 30 fps, 30–60 s, phone propped (add an explicit "prop your phone against something" onboarding step — handheld capture is the main failure). ROI = chest/shoulder region derived from a pose or face-mesh landmark, expanded downward. Chain: dense optical flow or per-frame ROI pixel-intensity/centroid signal → detrend → bandpass 0.1–0.7 Hz (6–42 breaths/min) → FFT peak plus zero-crossing cross-check. Reject if the ROI's global motion energy exceeds a threshold (user moved / someone walked behind). Quote ±1 breath/min. Product framing: measure RR, then run a 3-minute guided 6-bpm breathing exercise, then re-measure and show the drop — that visible before/after is the single most demo-able moment available to this product, and it is scientifically honest.

findings.claimOrFeature: Overnight ballistocardiography — phone on the mattress, accelerometer detecting heartbeat micro-vibrations
findings.reality: The published BCG evidence is for DEDICATED hardware — under-mattress piezo strips (EMFIT QS), air-mattress systems, bed-embedded sensors — not for a phone lying on a mattress, and even those report roughly 5 bpm average error. Phone-based cardiac vibration results that look good (SCG/GCG heartbeat detection sensitivity 89–97%, IBI limits of agreement ±5–7 ms) come from the phone placed ON THE CHEST of a still, awake, supine subject — a completely different mechanical coupling than a phone on a mattress metres of foam away from the sternum. Practical blockers stack up: memory foam and thick spring mattresses attenuate exactly the frequencies you need; a bed partner injects uncorrelated motion with no way to separate sources from a single 3-axis accelerometer; phone placement (under pillow vs beside body vs on nightstand) changes the signal completely and users will not comply; overnight accelerometer sampling at BCG-usable rates (100–200 Hz) plus continuous processing drains battery and heats a phone sitting in bedding, which is a genuine safety and 1-star-review risk; and on Android, Doze and background-execution limits fight you for the whole 8 hours.
findings.evidence: "An average error of about 5 bpm has been documented for mattress-based systems" — and those are dedicated under-mattress sensors. Phone-based figures ("sensitivity and PPV of 89.3%/93.3% in SCG and 97.3%/97.9% in GCG," IBI LoA ±7.33 ms SCG / ±5.22 ms GCG) come from chest-placed smartphone inertial units with the user still.
findings.correction: Cut overnight BCG heart rate. Replace with what phone accelerometers demonstrably CAN do overnight: actigraphy-grade sleep-window detection (bed time, wake time, gross movement/restlessness index), which is buildable with low-rate accelerometer sampling and survives Doze. Pair it with device-usage signals (last screen-off, first unlock) which cost nothing and are more reliable than the accelerometer for sleep/wake boundaries. Label it "Sleep window & restlessness," never "sleep stages" and never "overnight heart rate." If nocturnal heart rate is genuinely required by the PMOS thesis, that is a NEEDS-EXTERNAL-DEVICE requirement and violates the no-hardware constraint — say so in the spec explicitly rather than papering over it with BCG.

findings.claimOrFeature: Camera-based stress estimation from facial action units
findings.reality: This is not merely an accuracy problem, it is a construct-validity problem: the premise that an internal affective or stress state can be read off facial movements is rejected by the field's own major review. Barrett, Adolphs, Marsella, Martinez and Pollak (2019), a 68-page consensus review in Psychological Science in the Public Interest, concluded that facial configurations map onto emotion categories with limited reliability and limited specificity, and vary substantially across cultures, individuals and contexts — and specifically warned about the commercial applications built on the 'common view.' Layered on top: facial-expression models are trained overwhelmingly on Western datasets, and PMOS users in India will be a demographic the training data barely covers. Shipping a number labelled "stress" derived from face video is the kind of claim that draws both press criticism and App Store 1.4.1 scrutiny (accuracy claims that cannot be validated get rejected).
findings.evidence: Barrett et al. (2019), "Emotional expressions reconsidered: challenges to inferring emotion from human facial movements," Psychological Science in the Public Interest 20(1):1–68 — surveys the assumption that "a person's emotional state can be readily inferred from facial movements," finds significant cultural and individual variability, and explicitly flags the influence of this assumption on "commercial applications."
findings.correction: Delete facial-AU stress inference. Replace with a two-part substitute that is honest and still feels smart: (1) a 1-tap self-reported stress rating (single-item stress scales correlate acceptably with longer instruments and are the actual clinical practice), and (2) a physiological AROUSAL proxy from the already-validated fingertip PPG — resting pulse rate elevation and rMSSD depression versus the user's own 14-day baseline. Label the output "Your body looks more activated than your usual" (a physiological statement) rather than "You are stressed" (a psychological inference). This is defensible, uses signals you can actually measure, and is more useful for an n-of-1 engine because it is anchored to the individual.

findings.claimOrFeature: Voice biomarkers for mood from short voice clips, including Hindi and Tamil users
findings.reality: Cross-lingual transfer collapses to near chance. In cross-dataset experiments between the English DAIC-WOZ and Chinese MODMA corpora, training on one language and testing on the other yielded 48.72% accuracy — a coin flip on a binary task. Reviews of the field report methodological heterogeneity, small samples, non-comparable metrics, near-absence of longitudinal designs, unreported comorbidities, and demographic bias, and conclude generalisability must be addressed before clinical adoption. For this product specifically: there is no meaningful labelled Tamil or Hindi depression/mood speech corpus to fine-tune on, Indian-English accent variation is enormous, code-switching (Tanglish/Hinglish) breaks both acoustic and linguistic models, and phone-microphone/codec variability adds channel effects that models routinely learn instead of the target signal. Also note mood inference from voice sits close to the 1.4.1 "accuracy claims that cannot be validated" trigger.
findings.evidence: "When researchers conducted cross-dataset experiments between the English DAIC-WOZ dataset and Chinese MODMA dataset, accuracy was only 48.72% when trained on one language and tested on another"; "A key drawback of current models is their poor cross-lingual generalization; they often degrade sharply when applied to languages or real-world datasets other than the one used for training."
findings.correction: Cut voice-derived mood scoring from the roadmap. If voice is wanted as an INPUT modality rather than a biomarker, ship it as voice-note journaling: the user speaks for 30 seconds, on-device or server-side ASR transcribes it, and the text feeds the symptom log and an LLM-generated reflection. That is genuinely useful, works in Tamil and Hindi (Whisper-class models handle both), respects the no-hardware constraint, and makes zero inference claims. Explicitly write into the spec: "we do not infer emotional state from acoustic features."

findings.claimOrFeature: Cuffless blood pressure via pulse transit time from simultaneous face + finger PPG
findings.reality: The engineering is the easy part; the claim is the blocked part. Simultaneous front+rear capture IS possible — AVCaptureMultiCamSession (iOS 13+, A12 Bionic or later) and CameraX 1.3+ / Camera2 concurrent streaming on Android (capped at 720p or 1440p per stream, 2 or fewer UseCases per camera), and a 2025 dual-view smartphone PPG dataset (M3PD, 60 participants) exists. But: Apple Guideline 1.4.1 names blood pressure explicitly as not permitted using only device sensors, so it cannot ship on iOS at all. Scientifically, the ESH 2023 guidance recommends against cuffless devices in clinical practice on accuracy grounds and notes no generally accepted validation protocol exists (ISO 81060-7 is still being developed); AAMI/ESH/ISO 81060-2 explicitly should not be used to validate a cuffless device. Uncalibrated PTT-BP is not valid: vessel diameter and distensibility affect pulse wave velocity independently of BP, and autonomic state alone can shift the estimate by more than 10 mmHg. Enforcement is live — FDA issued a warning letter to WHOOP on 14 July 2025 over Blood Pressure Insights being marketed without clearance, on a device with far better sensors than a phone camera.
findings.evidence: Apple 1.4.1: "...measure blood pressure... using only the sensors on the device are not permitted." ESH 2023: cuffless devices "heterogeneous in measurement principle, intended use, functions, and calibration" with "special accuracy issues"; "to date, there are no generally accepted protocols for their validation." FDA warning letter to WHOOP, 14 July 2025, stating Blood Pressure Insights was "neither cleared nor approved" and qualifies as a medical device.
findings.correction: Cut BP estimation. Do not soften it to "BP trend," "BP index," or "cardiovascular load score" — the FDA/WHOOP letter shows that renaming a BP-adjacent output does not avoid device classification. Keep the multi-camera capability in the spec only for a legitimate non-BP use: dual-view PPG (face + finger simultaneously) measurably improves heart-rate robustness — the M3PD paper reports 21.9–30.2% heart-rate error reduction over single-view baselines — so use both cameras to make the HR reading more robust and to cross-validate the finger reading against the face reading as a quality gate. That is a genuinely impressive, defensible demo that uses the same hardware trick without touching a regulated claim. Gate it on AVCaptureMultiCamSession.isMultiCamSupported / getAvailableConcurrentCameraInfos() with graceful single-camera fallback.

findings.claimOrFeature: Acne severity scoring from selfies
findings.reality: The most technically achievable of the vision features, but not at clinician-grade and not with a general multimodal model. Purpose-trained models on the ACNE04 benchmark reach roughly 84–87% severity-grading accuracy, and a smartphone-image production pipeline (Faster R-CNN lesion detection + LightGBM IGA grading) reported mAP 0.54 for lesion detection and 0.85 mean accuracy for severity grading — note the detection mAP is the weak link, meaning lesion COUNTS are unreliable even when the coarse grade is roughly right. Skin-tone generalisation is a documented gap: most models are trained on predominantly Caucasian datasets and lack handling for post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, which is highly prevalent in Indian skin (Fitzpatrick IV–V) and is the exact feature a model will confuse with active lesions. A general-purpose multimodal LLM will give plausible-sounding but unstable grades — rerun the same photo twice and get different answers — which is worse than useless for a tracking product where consistency matters more than absolute accuracy.
findings.evidence: "The Faster R-CNN model achieves a mAP of 0.54 for acne object detection, and the LightGBM model achieved mean accuracy of 0.85 for severity grading"; "Most deep learning models have been based on Caucasian datasets, and models specific to patients with distinct skin characteristics, such as higher propensity for post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, are lacking."
findings.correction: Reframe from "severity score" to "consistent visual tracking." Ship: a guided selfie capture with a fixed on-screen face outline, a lighting-quality check that refuses the shot if too dark or backlit, front camera, flash off, and store the photo locally. The primary output is a side-by-side / time-lapse comparison the user reads themselves — that is the retention feature and it needs no model at all. Layer a 4-level coarse category (clear / mild / moderate / severe) on top only if you fine-tune on ACNE04 plus Indian-skin images and validate stability by re-scoring the same photo 10 times; ship the category only if it is stable. Never output a lesion count. Never claim to distinguish acne from other dermatoses. Add a fixed disclaimer plus the 1.4.1-required "check with a doctor" reminder.

findings.claimOrFeature: Hirsutism density scoring from selfies using a Ferriman-Gallwey-style scale
findings.reality: No validated automated mFG scoring system surfaced in the literature — searches for deep-learning Ferriman-Gallwey automation return only the manual scoring literature. Worse, the reference standard itself is poor: modified Ferriman-Gallwey has considerable interobserver discrepancy, with reported variability reaching 14 points and individual scores 60% higher or 46% lower between patient and physician. You cannot train a reliable model against a label that noisy, and you have no labelled dataset. Compounding this: mFG requires scoring nine androgen-sensitive body areas including chest, upper and lower abdomen, upper and lower back, and thigh — asking users to photograph these creates intimate imagery on a consumer app, which is a serious App Store/Play safety, privacy and India-market cultural problem entirely apart from the science. Fine terminal-hair detection also demands macro-level resolution and controlled lighting that handheld selfies will not deliver, and performance will vary sharply with hair colour contrast against skin tone.
findings.evidence: "The Ferriman-Gallwey scores have considerable interobserver discrepancy, with interobserver variability potentially reaching 14 points, where some scores could be as much as 60% higher or 46% lower between the patient and the physician." No published automated image-based mFG validation was found.
findings.correction: Cut automated hirsutism scoring. Replace with self-reported mFG: present the standard nine-area illustrated 0–4 scale as a guided in-app questionnaire the user completes herself. Patient self-scoring is already established practice and is exactly what the cited concordance literature studies; it needs no camera, no model, no intimate photography, and produces a legitimate longitudinal number for the n-of-1 engine. Optionally allow a private, on-device-only, user-initiated photo of a single non-intimate area (chin/upper lip) purely as a visual diary with no scoring — same pattern as the acne feature. Explicitly state in the spec that no body imagery leaves the device.

result.headline: The Nature paper is real and the accuracy numbers are real — but PHRM is a Google-internal research system released under a non-commercial, non-clinical, IRB-gated licence with no SDK, and the "8-second clip captured automatically on phone unlock" trigger is flatly impossible for a third-party app on Android, iOS AND web. The entire v2 pillar must be rewritten from "passive on unlock" to "user-initiated foreground 30-second selfie check-in," and even then the study's own free-living success rate was 43% overall and 25% for the darkest skin tones — a fatal number for an India-first product.

findings.claimOrFeature: Spec cites Nature (June 2026) paper on Google PHRM at https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10507-6
findings.reality: The citation is GENUINE and correctly attributed. Liao, S., Di Achille, P., Wu, J. et al., 'Passive heart-rate monitoring during smartphone use in everyday life', Nature, published 2 June 2026, DOI 10.1038/s41586-026-10507-6. All 18 authors are Google Research employees; funded by Alphabet Inc. A preprint exists as arXiv:2503.03783v3 with the same title and author list. This is the one thing in the spec that survives scrutiny intact. What does NOT survive is the implied status: the paper describes a research system run by consented study participants under an IRB protocol, not a shipping capability.
findings.evidence: Nature paper metadata confirmed via DOI 10.1038/s41586-026-10507-6 and mirrored arXiv preprint 2503.03783v3. Google's own blog calls it 'a research system'. arXiv data-availability statement: 'The data that support the findings of this study are not openly available due to reasons of study participant privacy.' Code availability: 'A pseudocode implementation of the algorithms is available in the Supplementary Materials' — not full source.
findings.correction: Keep the citation but change the verb. Replace 'PHRM enables…' with: 'Google Research demonstrated in Nature (Liao et al., 2026, DOI 10.1038/s41586-026-10507-6) that smartphone-camera rPPG can reach wearable-grade daily RHR accuracy under study conditions. This validates the SCIENCE of camera rPPG. It does not give us the CAPABILITY — see platform findings below.'

findings.claimOrFeature: v2 pillar assumes PHRM is available to us as an SDK / API / ML Kit feature / Health Connect data type
findings.reality: There is NO PHRM SDK, API, ML Kit feature, Health Connect type, or Android system service. ML Kit's full API surface is: barcode, face detection, face mesh, text recognition, image labeling, object detection, digital ink, pose, selfie segmentation, subject segmentation, document scanner, plus NLP and Gemini Nano GenAI APIs. Zero vitals/rPPG/PPG APIs. Health Connect exposes HeartRateRecord and RestingHeartRateRecord as STORAGE SCHEMAS you can read/write — it is a data bus, not a sensor. Health Connect will happily store a heart rate you compute; it will never produce one from a camera. There is no Google-provided path from front camera to bpm for a third party.
findings.evidence: ML Kit product listing enumerates all available APIs with no vital-signs entry. Google's PHRM blog announces only a dataset, a pre-trained 'PHRM-mini' model, and code — no product, SDK, or API, and no stated productization plan. Health Connect docs describe it as a unified local data store aggregating from Wear OS, Samsung Health, Fitbit, Garmin and other apps.
findings.correction: Delete every reference to 'PHRM' as a thing we integrate. Rewrite as: 'We implement our own camera rPPG using a licensed third-party SDK or an in-house model. Google's PHRM is not available to third-party developers in any form; we write our resulting HR values INTO Health Connect (HeartRateRecord / RestingHeartRateRecord) rather than reading them out.'

findings.claimOrFeature: Spec implies we can use Google's released PHRM-mini pre-trained model and dataset
findings.reality: The released artefacts are explicitly and exclusively barred from commercial use. The Google Heart Rate Measurement Study Dataset and the PHRM-mini model are 'available to qualified researchers for non-commercial, non-clinical research use only.' Access requires: a Google Forms application, a verified institutional academic email, documented IRB approval for the research protocol, a data-security plan, and an attestation. Redistribution to third parties is prohibited. A 4-person commercial startup shipping a consumer app on Play/App Store cannot lawfully qualify for, obtain, or use these weights. Note the double bar: 'non-commercial' kills the business model AND 'non-clinical' kills the health framing.
findings.evidence: Repo terms: 'The HR Dataset is available solely for research purposes and is not intended for commercial use'; users must agree not to use it 'for any purpose other than non-commercial, non-clinical research purposes'; must not share with third parties or re-identify individuals; access via IRB-gated application to google-heart-rate-measurement-study@google.com.
findings.correction: Remove PHRM-mini from the architecture entirely. Add an explicit line to the risks register: 'PHRM-mini weights and the Google HR dataset are licensed for non-commercial, non-clinical academic research with IRB approval. We cannot use them. Any rPPG capability must come from a commercially-licensed SDK or a model we train on data we have rights to.'

findings.claimOrFeature: 'Front-camera 8-second rPPG clip captured automatically on phone unlock' — Android
findings.reality: Three independent Android restrictions each kill this on their own. (1) Android 14 (API 34): 'You cannot create a camera foreground service while your app is in the background' — CAMERA is a while-in-use permission, so the OS throws SecurityException when a backgrounded app starts an FGS of type camera. (2) Android 10 (API 29)+ background activity start restrictions mean an unlock event cannot bring your capture UI to the foreground; exceptions require a visible window, SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW, or a system-sent PendingIntent. (3) ACTION_USER_PRESENT is NOT on the implicit-broadcast exception list, so from Android 8.0 a manifest-declared receiver will not even be woken by an unlock. There is no supported way for a third-party Android app to observe unlock and silently open the front camera. Google's own study did not do this covertly either: participants installed a bespoke research app under consent, clips were saved locally, and 'participants then reviewed the videos and manually authorized upload.'
findings.evidence: developer.android.com FGS background-start restrictions: camera FGS cannot be created from background; developer.android.com background-starts: activity starts from background blocked since API 29; broadcast-exceptions list contains BOOT_COMPLETED, TIME_SET, LOCALE_CHANGED, SMS_RECEIVED etc. — USER_PRESENT and SCREEN_ON are absent. arXiv:2503.03783v3 describes a custom consented data-collection app with manual upload authorisation.
findings.correction: Replace 'captured automatically on phone unlock' with: 'User-initiated foreground check-in. The app schedules a notification (e.g. morning + evening); tapping it opens the app to a full-screen capture view with the camera preview visible, the user holds still for ~30s, and we compute HR on-device. Passive-on-unlock is impossible for any non-OS-vendor app on Android and is removed from scope permanently, not deferred to a later version.'

findings.claimOrFeature: Same passive-on-unlock capture on iOS
findings.reality: Harder-blocked than Android. iOS exposes NO unlock event to third-party apps at all — there is no equivalent of ACTION_USER_PRESENT, so the trigger itself does not exist. Separately, camera capture stops the moment the app leaves the foreground: AVCaptureSession reports interruption reason videoDeviceNotAvailableInBackground. isMultitaskingCameraAccessSupported is true only for iPads with Stage Manager, for apps declaring the 'voip' UIBackgroundMode, or for apps granted the com.apple.developer.avfoundation.multitasking-camera-access entitlement, which must be requested from and approved by Apple — a wellness app claiming VoIP background mode to run a camera would be rejected under App Review. Finally, the green camera privacy indicator has been mandatory and non-suppressible since iOS 14, so even a hypothetical bypass is user-visible.
findings.evidence: Apple developer documentation for AVCaptureSession.InterruptionReason.videoDeviceNotAvailableInBackground; AVCaptureSession.isMultitaskingCameraAccessSupported requirements (iPad Stage Manager, voip background mode, or Apple-granted multitasking-camera-access entitlement); iOS 14+ camera/mic indicator dots cannot be disabled.
findings.correction: State plainly in the spec: 'iOS provides no unlock hook and no background camera access for apps of this category. The capture flow is identical on both platforms: notification → user taps → foreground capture screen. Do not write any iOS-specific passive path; there is none to write.'

findings.claimOrFeature: PWA fallback for the same passive rPPG capture
findings.reality: The web is the most restricted of the three, not the escape hatch. getUserMedia() requires a secure context, an explicit per-origin permission prompt, and (per current browser behaviour and the W3C mediacapture-extensions discussion) a user gesture. Mobile browsers release or suspend the camera when the page is backgrounded or the screen locks, and iOS Safari in particular tears down media tracks aggressively on visibility change. A PWA also has no way to know the phone was unlocked. Additionally the PWA route forces the frames somewhere: on-device rPPG in WASM/JS is materially slower and less accurate than native, and shipping frames to a cloud API creates a face-biometrics transfer that is a live problem under India's DPDP Act.
findings.evidence: MDN MediaDevices.getUserMedia(): available only in secure contexts, 'must always get user permission before opening any media gathering input'; W3C mediacapture-extensions issue #11 on enforcing user gesture; long-standing browser behaviour of holding/releasing the camera lock when the browser is backgrounded (Bugzilla 874572).
findings.correction: If the PWA stays in scope, scope it down explicitly: 'PWA supports manual, in-session capture only, while the tab is visible and focused. Any camera measurement in the PWA is a tap-to-measure flow. No background, no unlock trigger, no scheduled capture.'

findings.claimOrFeature: Quoted accuracy: '<10% mean percentage error vs ECG' and '<5 bpm MAE for daily RHR'
findings.reality: Both numbers are REAL and correctly quoted, but they are ceilings from a controlled study, not floors we would inherit. Free-living: video-level MAPE 4.83% (95% CI 4.39–5.28), participant-level MAPE 6.09% (5.35–6.87), participant-level MAE 4.58 bpm vs ECG chest strap. Daily RHR: day-level MAE 3.62 bpm (3.18–4.09), participant-level MAE 4.39 bpm (3.67–5.17) vs Fitbit Charge 6. CRITICAL CONTEXT THE SPEC OMITS: these are computed only over clips that PASSED quality gating. In free-living, only 43.1% of clips yielded a valid measurement (68,307 of 158,471). In lab: 77.7% (1,360/1,750). Post-exercise success fell to 62.1% vs 78.4% at rest. Six participants were excluded outright for failing to produce 40+ clips on 3+ days. The <5 bpm RHR figure is also an artefact of AGGREGATION — Google averaged ~231 clips per participant per day. Our design will get 1–2 clips per day, so the RHR error will be far closer to the single-measurement MAE (~4.6 bpm and much worse tails) than to 3.62.
findings.evidence: arXiv:2503.03783v3 results: free-living video-level MAPE 4.83%, participant-level MAE 4.58 bpm; daily RHR participant-level MAE 4.39 bpm vs Fitbit Charge 6; free-living valid-measurement rate 68,307/158,471 = 43.1%; lab 1,360/1,750 = 77.7%; post-exercise success 62.1% vs at-rest 78.4%; app captured an average of 231 clips per participant per day.
findings.correction: Rewrite the claim as: 'Google reported free-living MAPE 4.83% and daily RHR MAE 4.39 bpm — but only on the 43% of clips that passed quality gating, aggregated over ~231 clips/user/day. Our design captures 1–2 clips/day, so we should plan for single-measurement error of roughly 5–8 bpm with a long tail, and we must never display a single reading as a precise number. Show trend bands, not bpm to the digit.'

findings.claimOrFeature: Implicit claim that PHRM works equally well for all users (India-first rollout)
findings.reality: This is the finding that should most worry an India-first product. Accuracy degrades on darker skin and, far more importantly, so does whether a measurement happens at all. Participant-level MAPE by Monk Skin Tone: MST 1–4 = 5.04%, MST 5–7 = 5.12%, MST 8–10 = 7.84%. Daily RHR MAE: 3.72 / 3.56 / 5.86 bpm — the darkest group MISSED the <5 bpm target and only converged below 5 bpm by day 3 of aggregation. But the buried number is the free-living VALID MEASUREMENT RATE by skin tone: 58% (MST 1–4), 45% (MST 5–7), 25% (MST 8–10). India's population sits predominantly in MST 5–8. Google also found MAPE was worst for the darkest group specifically under incandescent lighting, attributed to reduced spectral power at the green wavelengths rPPG depends on — i.e. indoor evening use in Indian homes is close to the worst case. Google's 'meets accuracy standards for all skin tones' claim is true only about the error on successful measurements; it says nothing about the 75% of attempts that failed for the darkest group.
findings.evidence: arXiv:2503.03783v3: free-living participant-level MAPE 5.04% / 5.12% / 7.84% for MST 1–4 / 5–7 / 8–10; RHR MAE 3.72 / 3.56 / 5.86 bpm; free-living success rates 58% / 45% / 25%; 'MAPEs were highest for the darkest skin tone group under incandescent lighting,' attributed to reduced spectral power in green wavelengths.
findings.correction: Add to the spec as a first-class design constraint: 'For our India-first user base (predominantly Monk Skin Tone 5–8), expect roughly 25–45% of camera measurement attempts to fail quality gating, worse under warm indoor lighting. The UX must treat failure as the normal case: no streak-breaking, no guilt copy, clear retry guidance (face a window, hold still), and every downstream feature must degrade gracefully to zero HR data. Budget engineering time for a lighting-quality pre-check before capture.'

findings.claimOrFeature: Assumption that a viable third-party rPPG SDK exists to substitute for PHRM
findings.reality: Yes — three credible commercial options exist, and all three confirm the same shape: a FOREGROUND, USER-HELD, STILL, WELL-LIT, 10–60 SECOND SESSION. None of them offers passive or background capture, which is the strongest possible evidence that the passive pattern is unavailable to third parties. (1) Binah.ai SDK: on-device, no internet needed, iOS 14+/iPhone XS and above, Android 10+, plus Chrome-mobile/Safari web; HR at ~10s, BP/respiration/stress at 35–60s; ISO 13485:2016 certified, FDA SaaMD 'in process' (not cleared). (2) NuraLogix Anura Core SDK: Android 7.1+, iOS; REQUIRES Camera2 FULL or LEVEL_3 — 'Platforms that only have Camera2 API LEGACY are not supported', which excludes a meaningful share of budget Indian Android devices; uses a DeepAffex Cloud module; distributed via private git under a commercial licence, sales contact required. (3) VitalLens (Rouast Labs): cloud API, reported MAE 1.57 bpm HR on a 422-person benchmark, and explicitly 'not a medical device and is not intended for the diagnosis, prevention, monitoring, treatment, or alleviation of any disease.'
findings.evidence: Binah SDK page: platform requirements and 'Heart rate reported at ~10 seconds, followed by blood pressure, respiration rate, and mental stress in 35–60 seconds', runs on-device with no internet connection. Anura Core SDK platform requirements: Android 7.1+, 'The platform must support Camera2 API, specifically with FULL or LEVEL_3 support. Platforms that only have Camera2 API LEGACY are not supported.' VitalLens API page disclaimer.
findings.correction: Replace the PHRM pillar with: 'Camera check-in, powered by a licensed rPPG SDK (evaluate Binah.ai first — it is the only fully on-device option, which matters for DPDP compliance and offline use). Interaction model: notification → tap → hold phone at arm's length, face well-lit, still, 30–60s. Add a device-capability gate at install: Anura requires Camera2 FULL/LEVEL_3, Binah requires iPhone XS+/Android 10+ — a material share of the India entry-level Android base will not qualify and needs a non-camera fallback path.'

findings.claimOrFeature: Unstated: cost and privacy model of a cloud rPPG API at consumer scale
findings.reality: Cloud rPPG does not survive consumer-scale unit economics or India privacy review. VitalLens pricing is per FRAME: Free 20K frames/mo, Developer $19/mo for 200K, Business $199/mo for 4M, prepaid $39 for 250K. An 8-second clip at 30fps is 240 frames; a 30-second capture is 900. At just 1 capture/user/day, 10,000 users = ~300K captures/month = ~72 MILLION frames/month, roughly 18x the top published Business tier. There is also no Android SDK — it is listed as 'on our roadmap' — which is disqualifying for an India-first launch. Binah's per-seat model is the mirror problem: reported at ~$30/user/year at 10,000 users and ~$12/user/year at 100,000. A free consumer wellness app in India cannot carry $12–30/user/year of COGS. Separately, any cloud path ships identifiable FACE VIDEO to an overseas processor, which is sensitive personal data handling under India's DPDP Act and a serious consent/localisation burden for a 4-person team.
findings.evidence: VitalLens API pricing page: Free $0 (20K frames/mo), Developer $19/mo (200K), Business $199/mo (4M), Prepaid Starter $39 (250K); 'Python Client, JavaScript Client, and iOS SDK are provided' with Android SDK 'On our roadmap'. Binah.ai pricing reported at ~$30/user/year at 10,000 users and ~$12/user/year at 100,000 users.
findings.correction: Add a vendor-economics section: 'Cloud per-frame rPPG (VitalLens) is economically impossible at consumer scale — 10K DAU at 1 capture/day exceeds the top published tier ~18x — and it has no Android SDK. Prefer an on-device SDK (Binah) and negotiate a flat or MAU-capped licence, not per-seat, before committing to the feature. If no acceptable commercial terms exist, fall back to open-source classic rPPG (POS/CHROM/G, available in vitallens-python and rPPG-Toolbox) and explicitly downgrade the feature from a number to a qualitative trend indicator.'

findings.claimOrFeature: Camera-derived heart rate shipped in a consumer app on Play/App Store under a non-diagnostic framing
findings.reality: Shippable, but with mandatory, non-negotiable obligations that the spec does not currently account for. Google Play's Health Content and Services policy requires: completing the Health apps declaration form in Play Console; disclosing device compatibility IN THE APP DESCRIPTION where sensor-based health functions are used (the policy's own example is oximetry apps that 'must properly disclose which device models can support the functionality' — directly analogous to our Camera2/iPhone-XS gating); a clear disclaimer that the app is 'not a medical device and does not diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any medical condition'; a reminder to consult a healthcare professional; and privacy policy links in both Play Console and the app. The policy also bars 'health and medical related functionalities that are misleading or potentially harmful' — quoting Google's <10% MAPE and <5 bpm figures as OUR accuracy, when we are not using Google's model or capture regime, is precisely the kind of claim that triggers this.
findings.evidence: Google Play Health Content and Services policy: health apps declaration form required; 'clearly state device compatibility information in the app description… apps with oximetry functionality using only device sensors must properly disclose which device models can support the functionality'; required disclaimer 'not a medical device and does not diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any medical condition'; must 'remind users to consult a healthcare professional'.
findings.correction: Add a compliance checklist to the spec: (1) Play Health apps declaration form; (2) store-listing device-compatibility disclosure naming the minimum Android/iOS and camera requirements; (3) in-app 'not a medical device' disclaimer and clinician-consultation reminder; (4) privacy policy in both places; (5) a hard rule that NO marketing or in-app copy quotes Google's PHRM accuracy figures as our own — we cite only accuracy we have measured on our own pipeline.

findings.claimOrFeature: Ambient risk: conflating Google's camera PHRM with Fitbit's FDA-submitted 'passive heart rate' AFib algorithm
findings.reality: 'Passive heart rate monitoring' is an overloaded term and the two things are unrelated. The FDA-submitted Fitbit passive-HR work (Fitbit Heart Study, reported ~98% accuracy for AFib detection) is WRIST PPG on a Fitbit wearable — it needs a purchased device and is a first-party Fitbit feature with no third-party developer access. Google's 2026 PHRM is CAMERA rPPG on the phone. If the spec's roadmap or investor deck leans on 'FDA-submitted passive heart rate' credibility, it is borrowing legitimacy from a wearable feature that the no-external-devices constraint forbids and that we could not access even with a wearable. Conversely, the camera PHRM has no regulatory clearance of any kind.
findings.evidence: Fitbit's passive heart rate monitoring algorithm (wrist PPG, AFib detection, Fitbit Heart Study launched May 2020, ~98% accuracy) submitted for FDA approval; first-party Fitbit feature, no mention of third-party developer access. Distinct from Liao et al. 2026 camera-based PHRM, which has no regulatory clearance and no product availability.
findings.correction: Add a glossary line: 'PHRM in this document means camera rPPG (Liao et al., Nature 2026) only. It is unrelated to Fitbit's wrist-PPG passive HR / AFib algorithm, which requires a wearable and is first-party-only. Neither is available to us. Never cite the Fitbit FDA submission as support for our camera feature.'

result.headline: The "no external devices" rule kills far less of the v2 "innovative" pillar than expected — only 2 of its 23 features (CGM sync, glucose-response meal tagging) are hard hardware dependencies, ~9%. The real casualty is elsewhere and quieter: v1's "Wearable import" line silently assumes a smartwatch, and it is load-bearing for sleep stages, HRV, resting HR and SpO2 that the Metabolic Weather card, phase-normalized baselines and the OSA screen all consume. Meanwhile CGM was already dead three times over independent of the device rule — Dexcom Stelo is not sold in India and is not in any announced expansion; Abbott's LibreLink has no official third-party API and no Apple Health/Health Connect write path, so every working integration violates the LibreView EULA; and the 2023 International Guideline names the 75g OGTT (₹100–300 in India) as the most accurate glycaemic test, not CGM (~₹8,400/month). Delete CGM from the spec entirely and reframe wearable data as "optional enrichment if already present," never as a v1 input.

findings.claimOrFeature: §3.14 / §4 Phase 2 / §5.4: "CGM / OTC glucose sync — Import from Dexcom Stelo, Abbott Libre, Apple Health" (v2, P1)
findings.reality: Dexcom Stelo is a US-only over-the-counter biosensor. Dexcom's own June 2026 investor announcement states international expansion is planned for the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand and South Korea 'beginning later this year and continuing into 2027.' India is not named in any announced Stelo market. Stelo is also absent from Dexcom's developer API supported-product list (which names G6, G7, G7 15-day, Dexcom ONE and ONE+). So the spec names, as a v2 P1 data source for an India-first product, a device that (a) cannot be purchased in India and (b) has no documented developer integration path anywhere.
findings.evidence: Dexcom press release: Stelo expansion to "the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand and South Korea beginning later this year and continuing into 2027" — India absent. Dexcom developer docs supported sources: "Dexcom G6®, G7®, G7 15-day, Dexcom ONE and Dexcom ONE+" — Stelo not mentioned.
findings.correction: Delete every mention of "Dexcom Stelo" from §3.14, §4 Phase 2, §5.4, §6.2 (node E2) and §6.8 (consent C6). It is not a shippable integration for an India-first product and naming a US-only OTC sensor in an India deck is a factual error a judge or investor can catch in one search.

findings.claimOrFeature: CGM affordability for a "mass-market Indian well-being app" (Abbott FreeStyle Libre, the only realistically available CGM in India)
findings.reality: The current India product is FreeStyle Libre 2 Plus (launched India Aug 2025), a 15-day wear sensor. Indian retail listings cluster at ₹3,420–₹5,249 per sensor (Moglix ₹4,349; Collateral Medical ₹4,448; IndiaMART Bengaluru ₹4,200). Continuous wear = ~2 sensors/month = ₹8,400–₹8,900/month. India's per-capita net national income (FY2024-25 NSO provisional) is ₹2,05,324/year ≈ ₹17,110/month. A CGM habit therefore costs roughly half of average per-capita monthly income — for a non-diabetic wellness user, indefinitely. This is not a 'grey zone optional import'; it is a purchase the product would be implicitly recommending.
findings.evidence: Abbott India press release: Libre 2 Plus "can be worn on the back of the arm for up to 15 days," launched across India Aug 2025. Retail: ₹4,349 (Moglix), ₹4,448 (Collateral Medical), ₹4,200 (IndiaMART Bengaluru Apr 2026). NSO: per-capita net national income ₹2,05,324 (FY2024-25).
findings.correction: Move CGM from a product feature to an explicitly-labelled 'Out of scope — external hardware' section, with the cost stated: "CGM costs ~₹8,400/month in India, ~50% of average per-capita monthly income. We do not build features that require it." This is a stronger pitch line than pretending to support it.

findings.claimOrFeature: Assumption that Abbott Libre data can be imported (via Apple Health or otherwise) by a third-party app
findings.reality: Abbott publishes no official third-party developer API for Libre. The FreeStyle LibreLink app does not declare Apple Health integration, and there is no documented Health Connect write path. Every functioning third-party Libre integration (Thryve, GlucosePhone, FLwatch, community projects) is built on reverse-engineered LibreView/LibreLinkUp endpoints — and the LibreLinkUp EULA expressly forbids this: §6.6 bars users from "reverse engineer, decompile, disassemble, decode, create derivative works of, gain access to the source code, or modify LibreView"; §6.4 bars "accessing LibreView through any automated means, including but not limited to scripts or web crawlers." So even for a user who already owns a Libre, the import path is either non-existent (official) or contractually prohibited (unofficial). A health app shipping on an EULA-violating scraped API is an existential legal risk for a 4-person team.
findings.evidence: LibreLinkUp App EULA (2025-05-27) §6.4 and §6.6, quoted above. The public 'libreview-unofficial' API documentation is explicitly "not affiliated with Abbott Diabetes Care, Inc."
findings.correction: Remove "Abbott Libre" as a named integration. If a CGM-owning user is ever supported, the only defensible mechanism is manual CSV import of a LibreView export that the user downloads herself — a user-initiated data-portability action, not an API. Label it Later/P3, single-digit user count, not v2/P1.

findings.claimOrFeature: Assumption that Dexcom CGM data is available to this app via the Dexcom API
findings.reality: Dexcom's API is gated. Sandbox is open (simulated accounts only). 'Limited Access' — the first tier touching real data — permits up to 5 authorized production users and requires an application plus a signed Data Licensing Agreement. Commercial deployment requires 'Full Access', which requires a questionnaire, a technical review by Dexcom, and a commercial review by Dexcom's Strategic Partnerships team, plus becoming an authorized Digital Health Partner with a continuing obligation to maintain at least one active Dexcom user within 60 days of public launch. A hackathon team cannot demo real Dexcom data beyond 5 accounts, and cannot ship it to consumers without a signed partnership.
findings.evidence: Dexcom developer docs, Scopes & Access: Limited Access "permits up to 5 authorized users"; Full Access "requires technical and commercial review by Dexcom's Strategic Partnerships team."
findings.correction: If CGM survives at all, the spec must state the gate explicitly: "Dexcom API = 5-user cap without a signed partnership; not shippable by us." Do not put a partnership-gated API behind a v2 P1 tag in a roadmap.

findings.claimOrFeature: Clinical justification for CGM in PMOS — "Makes invisible insulin resistance visible day-to-day" (§3.14, cites an ENDO 2025 CGM-feasibility abstract)
