findings.reality: The 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline — the spec's own primary clinical anchor — recommends the 75g OGTT as the most accurate test to assess glycaemic status in PCOS/PMOS regardless of BMI, with fasting glucose and/or HbA1c as reduced-accuracy fallbacks. CGM appears nowhere as a recommended assessment. The spec's supporting citation is a conference abstract (ENDO 2025, jendso supplement) plus a pilot study — feasibility-grade evidence, not a recommendation. So the single most expensive and most hardware-dependent feature in the document is also the least guideline-anchored. An OGTT at Thyrocare costs ₹100–₹300; a month of CGM costs ~₹8,400. The cheap option is the one the guideline actually endorses.
findings.evidence: 2023 Guideline recommendation: "the 75-g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) [is] the most accurate test to assess glycaemic status in PCOS, regardless of BMI"; fasting glucose/HbA1c only "if an OGTT cannot be performed... noting significantly reduced accuracy." Thyrocare GTT (2 hour) listed at ₹100; 75g GTT ₹300.
findings.correction: Replace the CGM feature with a guideline-aligned, zero-hardware substitute: an "OGTT readiness + result-logging" flow (already half-present as §3.6 'OGTT reminder + prep guide'). Reframe the pitch line from "we make insulin resistance visible daily" to "we make sure the one test that actually measures it gets done, prepped for, and tracked over years" — which is both cheaper and more defensible.

findings.claimOrFeature: §3.3 "Wearable import — Apple Health / Google Fit / Samsung Health sync: sleep stages, steps, resting HR, HRV, SpO₂" (v1, P1)
findings.reality: Of those five data types, only steps are producible by a phone alone. iPhone alone records time in bed, not sleep stages; sleep stages (Awake/REM/Core/Deep), resting heart rate and HRV all require an Apple Watch. The same holds on Android: Health Connect is a data layer, not a sensor — it contains sleep stages, RHR, HRV and SpO₂ only if some wearable wrote them. The spec tags this v1/P1 and then makes downstream v1 features depend on it: 'Phase-normalized HR/HRV baselines' (v1), 'Sleep regularity tracking' (v1), 'Overnight HR trend (wearable)' (v2), and §5.4 lists 'Sleep stages — Wearable import — v1' as a named signal. This is a silent hardware assumption sitting inside the v1 milestone, not a v2 nice-to-have.
findings.evidence: Apple Support: "iPhone... can only track time in bed while the Apple Watch tracks time asleep (Awake, REM, Core, Deep sleep)"; resting heart rate is computed by Apple Watch from all-day heart rate sampling.
findings.correction: Retag wearable import as "Optional enrichment — Later/P3, zero features depend on it." Rewrite the v1 line to: "Steps/movement from phone pedometer (CMPedometer / Health Connect StepsRecord) — phone-only." Substitute the phone-only path for the rest: resting HR from the active finger-PPG check (§3.3, already v1/P1), sleep timing from user-declared bed/wake plus the circadian unlock-timestamp proxy, and delete sleep *stages* entirely — no phone-only substitute exists and none is needed for the coaching lever, which is regularity, not architecture.

findings.claimOrFeature: "Google Fit" named as a sync target in §3.3, §6.2 (node E1) and §6.8 (consent C6)
findings.reality: Google Fit APIs are being retired. Google blocked all new developer sign-ups on 1 May 2024 — a team starting this product in 2026 literally cannot obtain Google Fit API access. Existing access is supported only until the end of 2026, and Google states there is no direct replacement for the Fit REST API. The correct targets are Health Connect (Android-only, on-device) and Apple HealthKit (iOS); for cloud/web there is no equivalent. Shipping a spec in July 2026 that names Google Fit as a v1 integration is naming a platform that will be dead before v1 ships.
findings.evidence: Android Developers, Google Fit migration FAQ: "Developers cannot sign up to use these APIs as of May 1, 2024"; "Google Fit APIs will be supported until the end of 2026"; "there's no direct replacement for the Fit REST API."
findings.correction: Global find-and-replace: "Apple Health / Google Fit / Samsung Health" → "Apple HealthKit (iOS) / Health Connect (Android)". Add the platform asymmetry note the spec currently hides: Health Connect is Android-only and has no web/PWA equivalent, so the PWA distribution channel gets zero wearable data by construction.

findings.claimOrFeature: Implicit assumption that reading sleep/HRV/SpO₂ from the platform health store is a routine integration for a 4-person team
findings.reality: Health Connect read access is not self-serve. Every data type must be declared and justified in a Play Console 'Health apps' form on the App content page, and access to sensitive types requires approval — apps that skip this are blocked at runtime. Google's guidance requires requesting only what supports a specific user-facing feature and documenting the reason per data type. Policy tightened further: the August 2025 Health policy update made the Health Apps Declaration mandatory, and January 2026 enforcement added a 'Medical Device' labeling system and stricter Health Connect data justifications. An app that reads HRV/SpO₂ and then shows an OSA screen and a 'Metabolic Weather' state is exactly the profile that draws reviewer scrutiny on the medical-device question.
findings.evidence: Android Developers, Declare access to Health Connect data types: "you must declare your app's data use as well as declare access to the Health Connect data types that your app uses. Users might be prompted with an error message where your app can't access the Health Connect data types because they require special approval." Play Console Health apps policy, Jan 2026 enforcement adds medical-device labeling.
findings.correction: Add a row to §9 Regulatory & Safety Guardrails: "Play Console Health Apps Declaration + per-data-type Health Connect justification is a gating dependency on any release that reads platform health data; budget 2–4 weeks of review latency and a possible rejection." And prefer requesting the narrowest set (steps only) precisely to avoid the medical-device labeling trap.

findings.claimOrFeature: Wearable import as a realistic data source for the stated primary user: Indian women 16–35
findings.reality: India's wearable market is contracting, and the part of it that grew is the part that produces the least trustworthy data. IDC: India wearables fell 4.0% YoY in 2025 to 114.2M units, with smartwatch shipments down 17.6% to 28.9M; Noise (26.6%), boAt (14.1%) and Fire-Boltt (9.7%) hold ~50%+ of smartwatch share, and the sub-₹5,000 price band grew its share 87%. These budget companion apps (NoiseFit, Fire-Boltt Fit) have no documented Health Connect integration — one Fire-Boltt app was pulled from Play in 2024 — so their data is often unreachable even if the user owns the watch. And where the data is reachable, sleep staging is the weakest output even on premium devices: PSG-validated studies find acceptable accuracy for total sleep time and sleep efficiency but limited capability for stage detection, with further degradation in insomnia and OSA populations — the exact population this product targets (37% OSA prevalence claimed in §2.2).
findings.evidence: IDC via BizTechReports: India wearables -4.0% to 114.2M units in 2025; smartwatch shipments -17.6% to 28.9M; Noise 26.6%, boAt 14.1%, Fire-Boltt 9.7%; sub-₹5,000 share +87%. SLEEP Advances PSG validation of six consumer wearables: sleep-stage detection capability "remains limited"; lower accuracy in insomnia and lower sensitivity in OSA patients.
findings.correction: Kill the competitive-matrix implication that wearable integration is a strength. Replace it with the honest positioning that is actually differentiating: "Works on a ₹10,000 phone with no watch, no sensor, no strips. Every competitor's metabolic layer needs hardware our user does not own." That is a better India-first pitch than a wearable checkbox.

findings.claimOrFeature: §3.6 "Home glucose log (optional) — CGM or glucometer readings correlated with meals/mood" (v2, P2)
findings.reality: A glucometer is cheap to acquire but not cheap to use: meters run ~₹500–1,500 and strips ₹8–15 each (Accu-Chek Active 50 strips ₹899; OneTouch Select 25 strips ₹395), with proprietary strip lock-in per brand. Meaningful post-meal glucose profiling needs several pricks per day — a recurring consumable cost plus a painful, adherence-hostile ritual for a non-diabetic wellness user. Marking it "(optional)" does not exempt it: §6.7's Metabolic Weather fusion and §3.14's 'Glucose-response meal tagging' both consume glucose as an input, so the optional feature is quietly load-bearing for two non-optional ones.
findings.evidence: Accu-Chek Active 50 strips ₹899 (Moglix); OneTouch Select 25 strips from ₹395; per-strip range ₹8–15 with proprietary strip/meter lock-in.
findings.correction: There is no phone-only substitute for a glucose value — say so plainly rather than substituting a fake one. Replace 'Glucose-response meal tagging' with 'Meal-archetype → symptom tagging': the AI meal snap classifies high-GL vs low-GL Indian meal archetypes (phone-only), and the n-of-1 engine correlates that against her self-reported 2–4h energy crash, craving and skin outcomes. Copy must change from "your glucose rose 40 mg/dL after this meal" (impossible without hardware, and a quasi-clinical claim) to "meals like this are followed by an energy dip for you, 7 of 9 times."

findings.claimOrFeature: Blood pressure — §3.6 screening ledger "BP annually" and §3.14 "Pulse transit time (PTT) BP trend" (Later, P3)
findings.reality: Two different things, and only one is a violation. (a) "BP annually" in the screening ledger is a reminder to have BP measured by a clinician/pharmacy — a referral, not a hardware dependency; acceptable, same category as labs. (b) PTT-based BP from dual PPG is research-stage and, framed as any kind of BP output, drifts straight into regulated territory. (c) Critically, the only consumer product that comes close — Samsung Health Monitor — is not a counter-example but proof of the barrier: it requires a Galaxy Watch AND recalibration against an upper-arm cuff-based monitor every 28 days, is first-party Samsung only (no third-party API), CDSCO-cleared as a regulated feature in India, and its availability varies by country. That is a two-device dependency plus a regulatory clearance a 4-person team will not obtain.
findings.evidence: Samsung support: "After you have calibrated your Galaxy Watch with an upper-arm, cuff-based blood pressure monitor... You won't need to use the cuff-based monitor again until the next calibration in 28 days." India rollout was via CDSCO clearance on Galaxy Watch 4/5/6 series.
findings.correction: Keep "BP annually" in the screening ledger, explicitly labelled "measured at a clinic or pharmacy — we do not measure BP." Delete the PTT BP trend row entirely rather than leaving it at Later/P3: an unclaimed research row in a spec becomes a promised feature in a deck, and BP is the single fastest way to lose the non-SaMD framing in §9.

findings.claimOrFeature: Lab tests (fasting insulin, OGTT, lipids, vitamin D, HbA1c) — §3.6 Lab vault, Guideline screening ledger, Test-request helper, Vitamin D test-then-correct
findings.reality: Ruling: labs are NOT a violation of the no-external-devices rule, and this is not a close call. The rule exists to stop the product from being unusable unless the user buys and operates hardware the product tells her to buy. Labs fail every prong of that test: (1) she buys a one-off service, not a device she owns and operates; (2) the tests are mandated for every PMOS patient by the 2023 International Guideline whether or not this app exists — the app is a reminder layer over pre-existing routine care, not a demand generator; (3) costs are one-off and low in India (fasting insulin ~₹800 at Dr Lal PathLabs; 75g GTT ₹300 and 2-hour GTT ₹100 at Thyrocare; 25-OH vitamin D ₹700–1,300, with free home phlebotomy collection widely offered); (4) decisively, the lab *features* deliver their full value to a user who never gets a single test — 'Test-request helper', 'Question scripts' and 'Building My Case' produce an advocacy artifact from zero lab data. Compare CGM, which produces literally nothing without a ₹4,349 purchase. Two caveats that must be written into the spec, or the ruling flips.
findings.evidence: 2023 Guideline mandates OGTT/glycaemic screening, lipids and BP for PMOS independent of any app. India pricing: fasting insulin ~₹800 (Dr Lal PathLabs listing); Thyrocare 2-hour GTT ₹100, 75g GTT ₹300, 25-OH Vitamin D (Total) ₹700–1,300 with free home collection.
findings.correction: Add an explicit ruling paragraph to §3.6: "Lab tests are referrals into routine guideline-mandated care, not a product hardware dependency. Two hard constraints follow: (a) no n-of-1 pattern, experiment verdict, coaching lever, insight, or doctor export may be gated behind any lab value — the Lab vault is optional enrichment and every downstream feature must degrade gracefully to zero labs; (b) 'Vitamin D test-then-correct' must never block the supplement education flow on a test result." Also promote 'Test-request helper' (currently MVP/P0) in the pitch — it is the highest-leverage feature in the entire document precisely because it costs the user nothing and needs no hardware.

findings.claimOrFeature: §3.14 "Metabolic Weather daily card — Fuses RHR + HRV + sleep + steps + glucose" and §6.7 fusion flow (7 declared input signals); plus "Confidence-gated insight fusion — surface pattern only when ≥2 signal types agree"
findings.reality: Under the no-external-device rule the fusion card loses 2 of its 7 declared inputs outright (Glucose CV — needs CGM; Sleep stages — needs a wearable) and degrades 2 more (RHR and HRV drop from continuous wearable sampling to sparse, opt-in, consent-gated phone PPG samples). What actually survives phone-only: phone step count, user-declared bed/wake regularity, self-reported energy/mood, probabilistic cycle phase, and intermittent camera/finger PPG. That is still enough for a daily state card — but the card must be rebuilt around those five, not around the seven currently drawn in §6.7. The knock-on matters more: 'Confidence-gated insight fusion' requires ≥2 independent signal types to agree, and once glucose and wearable sleep are removed, the count of genuinely independent phone-derivable signal types is thin enough that the gate will suppress most insights — which is correct behaviour but destroys the promised insight volume against the §10 target of >1.5 pattern reveals/user/week.
findings.evidence: Spec §6.7 declares inputs RHR, HRV, SLEEP, STEPS, GLUC, MOOD, PHASE; §5.4 sources 'Glucose variability — CGM import (Stelo/Libre)' and 'Sleep stages — Wearable import'; both are external-hardware-only per the findings above.
findings.correction: Redraw the §6.7 diagram with exactly the phone-derivable inputs: phone steps, declared sleep timing + circadian regularity, self-reported energy/mood, cycle phase, and opt-in PPG-derived RHR/HRV with confidence weights. Add a line: "Glucose and wearable sleep stages are not inputs; the card is defined without them." Then re-derive the §10 pattern-reveal targets from the reduced signal set instead of inheriting numbers computed against a seven-signal fusion.

findings.claimOrFeature: How much of the "innovative" v2 pillar (§3.14, 23 features) collapses when external devices are removed?
findings.reality: Less than the framing suggests — and this is the audit's most useful positive finding. Of the 23 rows in §3.14, exactly 2 are hard external-device dependencies (CGM/OTC glucose sync; Glucose-response meal tagging) = ~9%. Two more are degraded-not-killed (Metabolic Weather fusion; Confidence-gated insight fusion). The other 19 — PHRM passive HR, opportunistic re-sampling, finger PPG SpO₂, contactless respiratory rate, bedside BCG, snoring audio, camera stress, AI meal snap, skin biomarker AI, hirsutism density, voice biomarker, circadian score, smart nudge timing, HRV biofeedback, Gemini RAG, brain-fog proxy, PTT BP, federated learning, digital control arm — are all phone-only by construction. In the §4 Phase 2 ship list, 1 of 12 items dies (CGM sync). By contrast §3.3 Passive & Physiological Monitoring loses or degrades 3 of 8 rows (wearable import; overnight HR wearable; the wearable-fed portion of sleep regularity), and §5.4's signal table loses 2 of 12. So the device rule costs v1 more than v2. Caveat, stated plainly: this finding says only that the surviving v2 features need no hardware. Whether they are *reliable* is a separate audit — several (BCG, contactless rRR, camera stress, PTT BP, brain-fog proxy) are research-grade, and 'phone-only' is not the same as 'shippable'.
findings.evidence: Feature-by-feature classification of §3.14's 23 rows and §4 Phase 2's 12-item ship list against the hardware criterion, cross-checked with the CGM and wearable findings above.
findings.correction: Add a short subsection '§3.14.1 Hardware posture' stating: "21 of 23 innovative features require nothing but the phone. We removed the 2 that did not (CGM sync, glucose-response meal tagging). No feature in this product requires a purchase." Then move the device-dependent rows into §8 Anti-Features as item 14: 'No feature that requires buying hardware — no wearable, no CGM, no glucometer, no cuff.' Turning the constraint into a stated anti-feature is both honest and a stronger differentiator than the wearable/CGM checkboxes currently sitting in the §7 competitive matrix.

result.headline: The "non-diagnostic well-being companion" framing does not survive contact with India's own rules: CDSCO's 2026 MDSW guidance says general-wellness software "should not be making any reference to diseases or disorders or pathological conditions," and that software which measures/estimates/reports physiologic values "for medical or clinical purposes, including screening, diagnosis, monitoring, alerting" is NOT general wellness software — so an app named for PMOS/PCOS that scores PHQ-9, screens for OSA, and escalates a cycle-gap alert about endometrial risk is Software as a Medical Device in India (likely Class B–C, MD-5/MD-9 licence, ISO 13485, clinical evidence), not a wellness app. The instrument licensing is the easy part (PHQ/GAD-7 are free); the intended-use statement is the thing that will sink the roadmap.

findings.claimOrFeature: PHQ-4 / PHQ-9 / GAD-7 can be embedded in a commercial consumer app without licence fees
findings.reality: Correct. The PHQ family and GAD-7 were released by Pfizer for free public use in 2010 and the official distribution site states no permission is needed at all — including for commercial apps and for translation. There is no fee, no licence agreement, and no per-seat royalty. The only real obligations are to reproduce items verbatim (any reworded item voids the published psychometrics) and to keep the developer attribution line.
findings.evidence: phqscreeners.com: "All PHQ, GAD-7 screeners and translations are downloadable from this website and no permission is required to reproduce, translate, display or distribute them." Pfizer's 2010 release announced free public access to these instruments.
findings.correction: Spec can state flatly: "PHQ-4/PHQ-9/GAD-7 are free for commercial use, no licence required (phqscreeners.com)." Add an engineering constraint: item text and the four response anchors (0=Not at all … 3=Nearly every day) must be rendered verbatim and the 2-week recall window must be preserved; no adaptive shortening, no LLM paraphrasing of items.

findings.claimOrFeature: Validated Hindi and Tamil versions of the screeners are available for an India-first launch
findings.reality: Partly true, and the gap is exactly where the spec is likely to be thinnest. GAD-7 has official translations in Tamil, Hindi, Telugu, Malayalam, Kannada, Marathi, Gujarati, Punjabi and Urdu. PHQ-9 Indian-language coverage on the official site is narrower and Tamil is not reliably listed there (Tamil PHQ-9 psychometrics come mainly from Sri Lankan and Indian head-and-neck-cancer research cohorts, not from the official distribution). PHQ-4 has essentially no official Hindi or Tamil version at all — it is a 2009 ultra-brief scale whose published translations are European/East Asian.
findings.evidence: Official GAD-7 language list (distributed via ILAE from phqscreeners) includes Tamil, Hindi, Telugu, Malayalam, Kannada, Marathi, Gujarati, Punjabi, Urdu. No equivalent official Tamil PHQ-4 exists; PHQ-4 translation literature covers Spanish, German, Greek, Mandarin, Korean, Filipino, Persian, Polish.
findings.correction: Do not ship "PHQ-4 in Tamil/Hindi" as if it were validated. Construct the 4 items from the official Tamil/Hindi GAD-7 (items 1–2 = GAD-2) plus the official PHQ-9 (items 1–2 = PHQ-2) in the same language, and label it in-app as "PHQ-2 + GAD-2, official translations" rather than PHQ-4. Where an official PHQ-9 translation for a target language does not exist (verify Tamil at source before committing), either fall back to the language that does exist or budget a forward/back-translation with cognitive debriefing — that is a ~3-month, ~1 clinician-linguist workstream per language, not a sprint task.

findings.claimOrFeature: Epworth Sleepiness Scale as the daytime-sleepiness instrument
findings.reality: The ESS is not free for this product. It is copyright M.W. Johns 1990–1997, administered exclusively by Mapi Research Trust (Lyon), and a signed licence agreement is mandatory for every user, with a user fee payable by commercial users. Translations are separately controlled and separately priced by Mapi; electronic/ePRO implementation is licensed separately from paper. Pricing is quoted case-by-case and is not public — meaning the spec cannot even cost it without a Mapi request.
findings.evidence: epworthsleepinessscale.com/licenses: "A licence is required to use either the ESS or the ESS-CHAD… Some users of the ESS have to pay a licence fee, others do not," with all licensing and translations handled by Mapi Research Trust; a licence agreement must be completed by all users and "a user fee is required from commercial & funded academic users."
findings.correction: Remove ESS from the spec. It buys nothing the 2023 PCOS guideline asks for and adds a paid third-party dependency plus per-language translation fees. Replace with the Berlin questionnaire (see next finding), which is what the guideline actually names.

findings.claimOrFeature: STOP-BANG as the OSA screener in a phone-only app
findings.reality: Two independent problems. (1) Licensing: STOP-Bang is proprietary to University Health Network (Dr Frances Chung); the official questionnaire PDF carries "Proprietary to University Health Network" and UHN requires a licence for uses beyond education, including clinical and commercial/app use. (2) Construct: 3 of its 8 points cannot be obtained from a phone — BMI >35 kg/m2, neck circumference >41 cm (female), and treated hypertension — and one point is awarded for male gender, which is structurally unobtainable in an all-female PMOS cohort. A woman therefore has a maximum realistic score of 7, and the published "high risk = 5+" cut-point was not calibrated on that truncated instrument.
findings.evidence: Official STOP-Bang scoring PDF footer: "Proprietary to University Health Network. www.stopbang.ca"; scoring criteria require "BMI > 35 kg/m2", "neck circumference (17"/43cm in male, 16"/41cm in female)" and "Gender = Male?".
findings.correction: Drop STOP-BANG. If it is kept for any reason, the spec must (a) name UHN licensing as a pre-launch blocker with an owner and a date, and (b) state that self-reported BMI/neck circumference degrade sensitivity and that no cut-point may be displayed as a risk tier.

findings.claimOrFeature: OSA screening framed as part of the app's cardiometabolic-risk story
findings.reality: The 2023 international PCOS guideline names the Berlin questionnaire as the preferred simple screening tool, and explicitly says OSA screening should be done to identify and relieve symptoms (snoring, unrefreshing sleep, daytime sleepiness, fatigue contributing to mood), and specifically should NOT be undertaken with the intention of improving cardiometabolic risk, citing inadequate evidence of metabolic benefit from OSA treatment in PCOS. A spec that sells OSA screening as metabolic-risk reduction is contradicting the guideline it cites — which is separately a Google Play violation risk.
findings.evidence: 2023 guideline: screening "should not be considered with the intention of improving cardiometabolic risk, with inadequate evidence for metabolic benefits of OSA treatment in PCOS and in general populations"; "a simple screening questionnaire, preferably the Berlin tool, could be applied and if positive, referral to a sleep specialist can be considered." Google Play: "We don't allow apps containing misleading health claims that contradict existing medical consensus."
findings.correction: Rewrite the OSA feature as symptom-led, not risk-led: trigger only on user-reported snoring/unrefreshing sleep/daytime sleepiness, use Berlin, and phrase the output as "these answers are common in people who are later found to have a sleep problem — worth raising with a doctor." Delete any copy linking OSA screening to insulin resistance or cardiometabolic risk. Note Berlin also needs BMI and known-hypertension status, so it too degrades on self-report; and its copyright status (Netzer 1999, Ann Intern Med) is not an explicit public-domain waiver — get written permission from the authors/journal before shipping.

findings.claimOrFeature: The product is a non-diagnostic well-being companion and therefore outside CDSCO regulation in India
findings.reality: This is the single most dangerous assumption in the spec. CDSCO's Guidance Document on Medical Device Software (Doc No. CDSCO/MD/GD/MDSW/01/2026) carves out "General Wellness Software" but attaches two notes that the spec's feature set fails on both counts: the intended-use statement must not reference diseases or disorders, and any software estimating/reporting physiologic values for screening, monitoring or alerting about a condition is excluded from the wellness carve-out. An app branded for PMOS/PCOS that scores PHQ-9, runs an OSA screener, and raises an endometrial-risk alert is MDSW under MDR-2017, full stop — disclaimers do not change intended use, and CDSCO explicitly says intended use is read from "labelling details, including instructions for use manuals, websites, promotional material."
findings.evidence: CDSCO MDSW guidance, s.5.2 General Wellness Software: "(i) The intended use statement … should not be making any reference to diseases or disorders or pathological conditions. (ii) Software intended to measure, estimate, or report physiologic values for medical or clinical purposes, including screening, diagnosis, monitoring, alerting, or management of a disease or a disorder or a condition, shall NOT be considered as General Wellness Software."
findings.correction: Pick one of two doctrines and write it into the spec as a governing constraint. (A) True wellness: the app never names PCOS/PMOS/depression/OSA/endometrial hyperplasia in any intended-use, store listing, or in-app output; it logs and reflects patterns and says "talk to a clinician" without naming what to talk about. This is a much smaller product than the spec describes. (B) Accept SaMD: budget a CDSCO licence (see next finding), ISO 13485, and clinical evidence. There is no third path where you keep the disease-named screening features and stay unregulated.

findings.claimOrFeature: If it were regulated in India it would be a low-risk Class A registration
findings.reality: No. CDSCO's Table 2 for standalone MDSW classifies by (healthcare situation) × (significance of information). "Drive clinical management" includes "to triage or identify early signs of a disease or condition" — which is exactly what a screening flag does. For a serious condition that lands at Class B; but the guidance adds a note that standalone MDSW used by non-clinical users in a serious situation without specialist support may be treated as CRITICAL, which pushes it to Class C. A direct-to-consumer app with no clinician in the loop is precisely that case. Class C means a Central Licensing Authority MD-9 manufacturing licence, ISO 13485 QMS, clinical evidence and post-market surveillance — not a 4-person-team artefact. Only Class A non-sterile/non-measuring escapes licensing (registration only).
findings.evidence: CDSCO MDSW guidance Table 2 and note: "Standalone MDSW intended to be used by non-clinical users in a 'serious situation or condition' … without the support from specialized professionals, may be considered as a MDSW used in a 'critical situation or condition'." Also: "Class A (non-sterile and non-measuring) medical device is exempted from the Licensing requirements, only registration is required as per Chapter IIIB of MDR-2017."
findings.correction: Add a explicit line to the spec: "If any screening/flagging feature ships, the expected CDSCO class is B–C (MD-5 via State LA, or MD-9 via CLA), not Class A registration. Timeline 9–18 months, plus ISO 13485." If that is unacceptable, the screening features must be cut in v1 rather than deferred, because the class is set by the intended-use statement the app launches with.

findings.claimOrFeature: Camera-derived SpO2 (and camera-derived blood pressure) displayed in-app
findings.reality: Hard-blocked on iOS by an explicit, enumerated App Review rule — not a judgement call, not curable by a disclaimer, and it applies even if the app is framed as wellness. Apple names blood oxygen and blood pressure specifically among measurements that may not be derived from device sensors alone. Any spec line proposing phone-camera SpO2 or phone-camera BP is unshippable on the App Store, and given the no-external-devices constraint there is no fallback sensor.
findings.evidence: App Store Review Guidelines 1.4.1: "apps that claim to take x-rays, measure blood pressure, body temperature, blood glucose levels, or blood oxygen levels using only the sensors on the device are not permitted."
findings.correction: Delete camera-derived SpO2 and camera-derived BP from the spec entirely, at every tier (not "v2"). If sleep-disordered-breathing signal is wanted, it must come from questionnaire (Berlin) plus subjective sleep logging, with no oxygen-saturation number anywhere in the UI or the data model.

findings.claimOrFeature: Camera-derived heart rate and HRV as a passive-sensing signal
findings.reality: Not prohibited outright — heart rate is conspicuously absent from Apple's banned-measurement list, and both FDA's revised January 2026 General Wellness guidance and CDSCO's wellness carve-out permit outputting physiologic parameters provided no disease or condition is referenced. But Apple imposes an evidence burden that a 4-person team usually has not budgeted for: accuracy claims must be backed by disclosed data and methodology, and unvalidatable methodology is an explicit rejection ground. HRV in particular has no consumer-grade accuracy convention from a phone camera, and the moment HRV is presented as a stress/PMOS marker it references a condition and leaves the wellness carve-out.
findings.evidence: App Store Review Guidelines 1.4.1: "Apps must clearly disclose data and methodology to support accuracy claims relating to health measurements, and if the level of accuracy or methodology cannot be validated, we will reject your app." FDA's revised General Wellness guidance (6 Jan 2026) permits sensor-derived physiologic outputs absent disease references.
findings.correction: Keep camera PPG heart rate; drop HRV-as-a-health-marker. Ship HR with (a) an in-app methodology page citing the rPPG technique and a bench comparison you actually ran, (b) no accuracy claim you cannot evidence, and (c) zero linkage in copy between an HR/HRV number and PCOS, insulin resistance, stress disorders or anything else nameable. If you cannot produce a comparison dataset before submission, present HR as a relative trend without an absolute bpm claim.

findings.claimOrFeature: Cycle-interval sentinel: escalate on >90-day gaps / fewer than 4 bleeds per year for endometrial protection
findings.reality: Clinically sound, but mis-attributed — and the two halves come from two different documents. The >90-day threshold is in the 2023 international guideline, as an irregular-cycle definition (">90 days for any one cycle" from ≥1 year post menarche), not as an endometrial-protection rule. The "at least 4 bleeds a year" target traces to RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 33, which states it as good practice (Grade B) in the form "a withdrawal bleed at least every 3–4 months," noting intervals >3 months may be associated with hyperplasia. The 2023 guideline itself does not recommend routine endometrial screening; its named strategies are weight management, cycle regulation and regular progestogen therapy.
findings.evidence: 2023 guideline: "1 year post menarche >90 days for any 1 cycle." RCOG GTG-33: "It is good practice to recommend treatment with progestogens to induce a withdrawal bleed at least every 3–4 months" and "intervals between menstruation of more than 3 months may be associated with endometrial hyperplasia."
findings.correction: Rewrite the citation as: ">90-day cycle threshold per 2023 International PCOS Guideline (irregular-cycle definition); ≥4 bleeds/year per RCOG GTG-33 (2014), Grade B good-practice." Do not attribute the 4-bleeds figure to the 2023 guideline. Separately, the escalation copy must never name endometrial hyperplasia or cancer: naming it converts the feature into "identify early signs of a disease" for a critical condition under CDSCO Table 2 and lands the whole app in Class C. Ship it as: "Your cycles have been more than 90 days apart. Guidelines suggest discussing this with a doctor." Nothing about why.

findings.claimOrFeature: Teen-safe mode with passive sensing for under-18 users in India
findings.reality: Section 9(3) of the DPDP Act is an absolute prohibition, not a consent-gated one: a Data Fiduciary shall not undertake tracking or behavioural monitoring of children, and "child" means anyone under 18. Continuous passive smartphone sensing to infer sleep, activity, mood or cycle patterns is behavioural monitoring by any ordinary reading. Parental consent does not cure it — 9(1) (verifiable parental consent) and 9(3) are separate obligations. The Rule 12 / Fourth Schedule relaxations exist for classes such as clinical establishments and health professionals and for purposes such as emergency medical care; a consumer wellness app run by a 4-person startup is neither. Rule 10 additionally requires verifiable parental consent using government-issued identity or a Digital Locker Service Provider token — real integration work, not a checkbox.
findings.evidence: DPDP Act 2023 s.9(3): "A Data Fiduciary shall not undertake tracking or behavioural monitoring of children or targeted advertising directed at children." DPDP Rules 2025 (notified 13 Nov 2025) Rule 10 prescribes verification via "reliable details of identity and age" or "a virtual token mapped to such details, which is issued by an authorised entity," including a Digital Locker Service Provider.
findings.correction: Change teen-safe mode from "same product, gentler copy" to a categorically different product: 18+ hard age gate for the sensing product; for under-18s, manual-entry-only cycle logging with no passive sensors, no behavioural inference, no personalisation engine, no retention beyond the current entry, and no ads of any kind — plus DigiLocker-based verifiable parental consent before any processing. If the team cannot build the DigiLocker consent flow, the honest answer is to block under-18 registration outright and say so in the spec. Deadline anchor: full obligations bite 13 May 2027.

findings.claimOrFeature: Face images, voice recordings and mental-health responses are covered by a standard DPDP consent flow
findings.reality: Under-specified in two directions. DPDP 2023 deliberately abolished the "sensitive personal data" tier, so face images, voice and PHQ-9 answers get no special statutory treatment under DPDP itself — but the older IT Act s.43A SPDI Rules 2011, which DO classify physical/mental health condition, medical records and biometric information as sensitive and require written consent and stricter handling, are not repealed until DPDP s.44(2) commences on 13 May 2027. So both regimes apply concurrently today, and the spec appears to plan for neither. Additionally, a face-image pipeline that scores hirsutism or acne is not a privacy question at all — it is a diagnostic claim about a PCOS feature, which is SaMD under the CDSCO analysis above.
findings.evidence: DPDP Act 2023 s.44(2) has been notified to come into force on 13.05.2027; until then IT Act s.43A and the SPDI Rules 2011 (which enumerate "physical, physiological and mental health condition", "medical records and history" and biometric information as sensitive personal data) remain in force alongside DPDP.
findings.correction: Spec should commit to: (1) all face and voice processing on-device with no server upload and no retention of raw media — this removes the largest DPDP/SPDI exposure and is also the only credible story for consumers; (2) treat health responses as SPDI under the 2011 Rules until 13 May 2027 (explicit written/electronic consent, published privacy policy, withdrawal mechanism); (3) an itemised DPDP notice, erasure-on-request and 72-hour breach process built before the May 2027 cliff; and (4) explicitly rule out any face-derived hirsutism/acne scoring, or accept SaMD classification for it.

findings.claimOrFeature: Launching on the App Store and Play Store as a health app is a routine submission
findings.reality: There are concrete, enumerated gates. Google Play requires every developer to complete the Health apps declaration and, for anything declared a regulated medical device, to "provide proof of approval, clearance or certification by the relevant authority upon request" — meaning if you declare period tracking + mental/behavioural health but market screening, you are exposed to a proof request you cannot satisfy. Play also mandates a specific disclaimer for non-medical health apps and bans misleading health claims. Apple additionally requires medical apps to remind users to consult a doctor and to submit regulatory clearance documentation if it exists. Camera and microphone purpose strings must "clearly and completely describe your use of the data" — a generic string on a passive-sensing app is a common rejection.
findings.evidence: Google Play Health Content and Services: apps regulated as medical devices must declare this and "provide proof of approval, clearance or certification by the relevant authority upon request"; non-medical apps require the disclaimer that the app is "not a medical device and does not diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any medical condition." Apple 1.4.1: "Apps should remind users to check with a doctor in addition to using the app and before making medical decisions."
findings.correction: Add a launch-gate checklist to the spec: (a) the exact Play disclaimer string shipped verbatim in-app and in the store listing; (b) Play Health apps declaration completed as Health & Fitness (period tracking, sleep, stress) and NOT as Clinical Decision Support or Disease Management; (c) store copy scrubbed of "screen", "detect", "diagnose", "risk score", "PCOS test"; (d) per-permission purpose strings written per feature; (e) an Apple 1.4.1 "consult a doctor" reminder on every result surface. Treat ASO keyword choices as regulated copy reviewed by the same person who owns the intended-use statement.

findings.claimOrFeature: Mental-health screening ships without a defined crisis pathway
findings.reality: No store rule explicitly mandates a crisis hotline, which is exactly why teams skip it — but PHQ-9 item 9 asks directly about thoughts of being better off dead or self-harm, and shipping that item with no response path is both a review risk under Play's prohibition on apps that "expose users to harmful health content and services" and an obvious liability and press risk in an India-first consumer product. India does have a usable, free, government-run destination: Tele-MANAS, 24x7, toll-free 14416 / 1800-891-4416, operating in English and 20 regional languages across all states and UTs under MoHFW.
findings.evidence: Google Play Health Content and Services: "We don't allow apps that expose users to harmful health content and services." Tele-MANAS (National Tele Mental Health Programme, launched 10 Oct 2022) provides 24x7 toll-free support on 14416 / 1800-89-14416 in English and 20 regional languages.
findings.correction: Two options, pick one in the spec. (A) Use PHQ-8 (PHQ-9 with item 9 removed — a validated variant) if the team cannot commit to a crisis pathway. (B) Keep PHQ-9 and hard-code an interrupt: any non-zero item-9 response immediately halts scoring, suppresses the total score, and surfaces Tele-MANAS 14416 as a tap-to-call in the user's chosen language, plus an emergency-contact prompt. Do not display a severity band on the same screen as a positive item 9. Document this flow in the Play Health apps declaration.

result.claimOrFeature: Google Fit APIs for reading steps / sleep / HR on Android (passive activity/sleep/HR ingestion for the PMOS companion app, phone-only)
result.reasoning:
The auditor's FACTS are all correct; the LABEL is wrong. Every citation checks out — I re-fetched the migration FAQ and it says verbatim "Developers cannot sign up to use these APIs as of May 1, 2024", "Google Fit APIs will be supported until the end of 2026", and "There is no alternative to the Fit REST API" (https://developer.android.com/health-and-fitness/health-connect/migration/fit/faq). So Google Fit itself is genuinely dead and must be struck from the spec. But "PLATFORM-BLOCKED" means the platform forbids a third party from doing this. The platform does not forbid it — it renamed the door. Three refutations:

(1) STEPS ARE FULLY SHIPPABLE, PHONE-ONLY, TODAY — and do not touch Health Connect or its declaration at all. The Recording API on mobile is Google's own named replacement for the Fit Android API and is explicitly "accountless, meaning it does not require a Google Account to use the service, and data is stored on-device." It needs exactly one runtime permission, android.permission.ACTIVITY_RECOGNITION — no OAuth scope, no allowlist, no sign-up gate, no Play health review. Supported types are TYPE_STEP_COUNT_DELTA, TYPE_DISTANCE_DELTA, TYPE_CALORIES_EXPENDED (https://developer.android.com/health-and-fitness/recording-api). Below that sits an even harder floor: raw Sensor.TYPE_STEP_COUNTER via SensorManager, a bare AOSP motion sensor needing only ACTIVITY_RECOGNITION on API 29+, with zero Google Play services dependency — which matters for India-first shipping on non-GMS/low-end devices (https://developer.android.com/develop/sensors-and-location/sensors/sensors_motion). A 4-person team ships either in days. Calling this blocked is simply wrong.

(2) HEALTH CONNECT IS A NORMAL PUBLISHING GATE, NOT A BLOCK. It is preinstalled and non-removable as part of the Android system on Android 14+, and a Play Store app on Android 13 and lower, back to Android 9 / API 28 (https://developer.android.com/health-and-fitness/health-connect/availability). The Health Apps declaration is a form with per-data-type justification that is reviewed — the same class of gate as a camera or location justification — and Strava, MyFitnessPal, Samsung Health, Fitbit, Oura and many small indies clear it routinely (https://developer.android.com/health-and-fitness/health-connect/publish). READ_HEALTH_DATA_IN_BACKGROUND and READ_HEALTH_DATA_HISTORY are separately declared, and the app should be designed to degrade gracefully without them, but they are grantable to third parties. Friction, not prohibition.

(3) THE CROSS-PLATFORM-PARITY ARGUMENT IS BACKWARDS. iOS never had Google Fit; you always needed HealthKit, which is also on-device-only with no server-side pull. So Health Connect + HealthKit is exactly symmetric, not a parity loss — that has always been the architecture for this app class.

WHERE THE AUDITOR IS RIGHT AND I CANNOT RESCUE IT: the Fit REST API death is real and permanent. There is no server-side pull of Android health data by any vendor. Any spec line implying a backend cron that fetches user health data must be deleted. The only lawful shape is: native Android client reads locally, then uploads to your backend under explicit informed consent, encrypted in transit and at rest, disclosed in Data Safety (https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/12991134).

WHY THE FINAL VERDICT IS DEGRADED, NOT SHIPPABLE: Health Connect is a data BROKER, not a data SOURCE. It only contains what some other app or device wrote into it. Under the hard no-external-device constraint, an unwearabled user's Health Connect store contains steps (phone pedometer) and essentially nothing else. Sleep has no phone-native writer unless the user separately installs a sleep-tracking app. Heart rate has no writer at all — the Recording API explicitly does not support HR or sleep. So the three signals split: steps = genuinely shippable phone-only; sleep and heart rate = NEEDS-EXTERNAL-DEVICE in practice, and reading them via Health Connect will return an empty result set for the majority of the target India-first user base. The spec must not count sleep or HR as passive-sensed inputs. That is a data-availability failure, not a platform block, but it is just as fatal to any feature that assumes those streams exist.
result.workaround: Delete every reference to Google Fit; it cannot be signed up for and expires end of 2026, inside year one. Replace with a three-tier Android ingestion stack, all phone-only. Tier 1 (build first, no gates): passive step/activity via the Recording API, falling back to raw Sensor.TYPE_STEP_COUNTER for non-GMS and low-end Indian devices — ACTIVITY_RECOGNITION only, no Google account, no health declaration, no review. This is the one truly passive signal the product gets for free and it should carry the activity/energy dimension of the PMOS model on its own. Tier 2 (build second, behind a gate): Health Connect as an OPPORTUNISTIC ENRICHMENT layer, never a dependency — read steps/sleep/HR if present, show the feature only when data actually exists, and design every screen to be fully functional when the store is empty. Ship without READ_HEALTH_DATA_IN_BACKGROUND and READ_HEALTH_DATA_HISTORY initially so the first Play review is a narrow, easily-justified ask; add them later once you have a usage record. On iOS the mirror is HealthKit; both are on-device, so build one shared sync abstraction with a native reader per platform. Tier 3 for the missing signals: sleep becomes a 10-second morning self-report (bed time, wake time, a 1-5 restedness tap) rather than a sensed stream — for a non-diagnostic well-being companion tracking cycle-linked patterns, self-reported sleep timing is honest, zero-cost, and a signal users will actually accept giving. Do NOT attempt to synthesize sleep from accelerometer or phone-usage data, and do NOT ship camera-PPG resting heart rate as a passive stream — treat HR as out of scope for v1 rather than shipping a number you cannot validate. Architecturally: accept that all reads happen on-device in the client and sync up to your backend with explicit consent; there is no server-side pull and no workaround for that. Also record the 2026 sunset as a roadmap risk item, since Health Connect is the only forward path and the Fit bridge disappears entirely.

result.claimOrFeature: Passive on-unlock camera capture on iOS — the app silently opens the front camera when the user unlocks their iPhone, captures a short face video for rPPG/well-being signals, with no deliberate user action.
result.reasoning:
I tried to refute this and could not. The ruling is upheld, and it fails independently at four separate layers — each one alone is fatal, so there is no combination of clever engineering that rescues it.

1) THE TRIGGER DOES NOT EXIST (strongest new evidence). Apple DTS engineer Quinn "The Eskimo!" states flatly on the official developer forums: "There's no supported way to track the device lock state specifically." He also pre-emptively kills the workaround the spec would reach for: "Using the data protection state as a proxy for the device lock state is a mistake. There are numerous ways in which this can fail, with the biggest one being that it's a complete non-starter if the user doesn't have a passcode set on their phone." UIApplication.protectedDataDidBecomeAvailableNotification is a data-protection signal, not an unlock signal — it also stays available 10–40 seconds after lock, so it produces false positives, and it never fires at all for users without a passcode. In India-first markets with high rates of passcode-less devices, that is a large fraction of the user base. This is worse than the original audit said: it is not just "no ACTION_USER_PRESENT equivalent," it is Apple explicitly telling developers not to attempt it.
(https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/808006)

2) NO CODE IS RUNNING TO RECEIVE THE TRIGGER. Even granting a trigger, a suspended third-party app cannot execute at unlock. iOS background execution for a wellness app is limited to BGAppRefreshTask (opportunistic, system-scheduled, not event-driven) and silent push (best-effort, rate-limited, user can disable). None of these are unlock-synchronized, and none grant camera access.

3) THE CAMERA IS HARD-STOPPED IN BACKGROUND. AVCaptureSession raises videoDeviceNotAvailableInBackground the instant the app leaves the foreground. isMultitaskingCameraAccessSupported is gated to iPad Stage Manager, apps declaring the `voip` UIBackgroundMode, or the com.apple.developer.avfoundation.multitasking-camera-access entitlement. That entitlement has no public request process — Michael Tsai documented it as "a private process available only to those deemed worthy by Apple," historically granted to Zoom-class video conferencing. A 4-person wellness app will not get it. Declaring `voip` to run a camera is a direct violation of App Review Guideline 2.5.4: "Multitasking apps may only use background services for their intended purposes: VoIP, audio playback, location, task completion, local notifications, etc." That is a rejection, not a grey area.
(https://developer.apple.com/documentation/AVFoundation/AVCaptureSession/InterruptionReason/videoDeviceNotAvailableInBackground, https://mjtsai.com/blog/2021/05/07/private-ipad-camera-multitasking-entitlement/)

4) "PASSIVE" IS ITSELF NON-COMPLIANT, EVEN IF 1–3 WERE SOLVED. App Review Guideline 2.5.14: "Apps must request explicit user consent and provide a clear visual and/or audible indication when recording, logging, or otherwise making a record of user activity. This includes any use of the device camera, microphone, screen recordings, or other user inputs." Combined with the non-suppressible iOS 14+ green camera indicator, a capture that the user does not notice is definitionally against the rules. The feature's core selling point — invisibility — is the thing Apple prohibits.

REFUTATION ATTEMPTS THAT FAILED:
- Screen Time / DeviceActivity: DeviceActivityReport surfaces pickup data, but the report extension is severely sandboxed — no network, no shared containers, data flows in only and cannot be passed back to the host app. DeviceActivityMonitor only fires intervalDidStart/intervalDidEnd/eventDidReachThreshold (not unlock), has a ~6MB memory ceiling, requires the Apple-approved Family Controls distribution entitlement, and grants zero camera access. Dead end.
- Existing iOS "intruder selfie" apps (Security Alarm–AntiTheft, Who Touched My Phone, App Locker): I checked these because they appear to disprove the block. They do not. They present their OWN in-app lock/alarm screen and capture while that screen is in the foreground. They cannot hook the system unlock. They confirm the boundary rather than breach it.
- Signal quality is a second, independent blocker. Even the state of the art in phone rPPG — Binah Check and Anura — requires a deliberate ~30-second foreground hold with the user sitting still and their face framed. A 1–2 second incidental unlock glance at an arbitrary angle under arbitrary lighting would not yield a usable waveform even if iOS permitted it. So this is RESEARCH-ONLY on accuracy grounds too.

One correction to the original audit, in its favor: it framed the entitlement as merely "must be approved by Apple." It is worse — there is no public application route at all.

result.reasoning:

WHAT SURVIVES. Everything the auditor says about Fitbit is correct and should stay in the audit. Fitbit's PPG AFib algorithm is wrist PPG on a purchased Fitbit, validated in the 455,000-participant Fitbit Heart Study at ~98% PPG-detection correctness, and it is a first-party feature with no third-party developer access to irregular-rhythm notifications. WHY THE LABEL FAILS. NEEDS-EXTERNAL-DEVICE asserts that FDA-cleared heart-rhythm credibility is only reachable through purchased hardware. That premise is false as of 2024/2026:

Multicenter validation (npj Digital Medicine): accuracy 98.5%, sensitivity 96.3%, specificity 99.3%, 60-second fingertip-on-camera recording, phone only (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12635274/, https://www.fibricheck.com/fibricheck-receives-fda-clearance-for-its-digital-heart-rhythm-monitor/).
- PreemptiveAI Clinical SDK (K250233, Measure Labs Inc., cleared 13 Feb 2026) is an FDA-cleared SaMD SDK explicitly built "for integration into third-party mobile apps," Android/iOS, 30-second fingertip video PPG (https://fda.innolitics.com/submissions/CV/subpart-c%E2%80%94cardiovascular-monitoring-devices/DXH/K250233).
So a phone-only, third-party-accessible, FDA-cleared camera-PPG path demonstrably exists. Labelling this NEEDS-EXTERNAL-DEVICE would send the team to buy wearables — which is doubly wrong, since Fitbit's AFib output is inaccessible even if they did.

WHY IT IS STILL BLOCKED, FOR DIFFERENT REASONS. I am correcting the label, not rescuing the feature. Three hard blockers remain:
1. "PASSIVE" IS PLATFORM-BLOCKED, not device-blocked. Android 9+ states flatly that a backgrounded app "cannot access the microphone or camera" (https://developer.android.com/about/versions/pie/android-9.0-changes-all); iOS grants camera to foreground only. Both cleared products are ACTIVE spot checks (60s and 30s fingertip). A foreground service holding the camera + flash indefinitely is not a product. The word "passive" cannot survive a phone-only build under any framing.
2. BOTH CLEARED OPTIONS ARE PRESCRIPTION-ONLY. FibriCheck's IFU is "self-testing by patients who have been diagnosed with, or are susceptible to developing, atrial fibrillation," Rx use under HCP guidance; PreemptiveAI is Rx-only and its IFU explicitly EXCLUDES patients with suspected arrhythmias (it measures pulse rate, not rhythm). Embedding either turns a non-diagnostic PMOS wellness companion into a regulated SaMD with Rx gating — incompatible with the stated framing and out of reach for a 4-person team (plus CDSCO registration for India-first).
3. INDIA-FIRST EQUITY RISK. FibriCheck sensitivity falls from 96.3% to 79.6% for Fitzpatrick V-VI skin tones, recovered to only 93.8% via human technician over-read. A 4-person team cannot staff a technician review loop, and this is the majority skin-tone range for the launch market.

NET: the defect is a citation/credibility defect. The spec cites wearable-derived FDA credibility for a camera feature. The honest citations (FibriCheck, PreemptiveAI) prove phone-only clearance is possible but are Rx-only and active — so they cannot be cited as our regulatory status either. Either way the spec cannot claim FDA-anything.
result.workaround:
Ship an ACTIVE, user-initiated 60-second fingertip camera PPG spot check, framed strictly as general wellness — and delete the words "passive," "FDA," and "AFib" from the spec, roadmap, and investor deck.

Concretely: (1) Build or license camera rPPG for resting pulse rate and HRV (RMSSD/SDNN) only — no rhythm classification, no irregularity flag, no arrhythmia language, which is what keeps it a wellness feature rather than a DXH-class device. (2) The n-of-1 value for PMOS comes from TRENDS, not absolute accuracy: a daily 60s morning reading correlated against cycle-phase, sleep, and stress logs gives a defensible personal baseline without needing clinical-grade precision or any clearance. (3) Cite FibriCheck (K232804) and PreemptiveAI (K250233) ONLY as third-party evidence that smartphone-camera PPG carries real physiological signal — never as our own regulatory standing, and never alongside Fitbit. (4) If a user's readings look erratic, the only permitted response is a neutral "consider discussing with a clinician" nudge with no detection claim attached. (5) Validate on Fitzpatrick IV-VI early and publish your own signal-quality rejection rate; the 79.6% figure is the risk you inherit in India, and an honest "we could not get a clean reading" state is far safer than a silently wrong number.

Users accept this readily — finger-on-camera for 60 seconds is the exact gesture every existing pulse app already trains. What they will not accept, and what platform policy will not permit, is the phone measuring their heart while they are not holding it.

result.claimOrFeature: Wearable and CGM sync (smartwatch HR/HRV/sleep stages, continuous glucose, BP cuff) as spec features in a phone-only, no-external-device PMOS well-being companion built by a 4-person third-party team.

And on Android, shipping Health Connect reads now requires passing the Play Console Health apps declaration form with per-data-type approval, enforced since 5 Mar 2025 (https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/14738291, https://developer.android.com/health-and-fitness/health-connect/publish) — real review-risk cost for a feature the median Indian user cannot switch on.

ROUTE 2 — "replace the sensor with phone-only measurement." This is where the hard block is, and it is stronger than the auditor realized: it is not just accuracy, it is written platform policy. That is a categorical ban covering exactly the two things the spec wants — glucose and BP. Any camera/PPG-derived "glucose estimate" or "cuffless BP" feature is a guaranteed iOS rejection, independent of how good the model is. The FDA safety communication (Feb 2024) that no non-invasive smartwatch or ring has ever been authorized for glucose reinforces that this is a policy-and-safety wall, not an engineering gap (https://www.healio.com/news/endocrinology/20240222/fda-avoid-using-smartwatches-smart-rings-to-measure-blood-glucose).

ROUTE 3 — "phone-only for the non-banned metrics." This is the one partial win, and it should be extracted from the wreckage. HR and HRV are NOT on Apple's prohibited list, and contact PPG via rear camera + flash is shipping today in App Store/Play apps (HRV4Training, Welltory) with peer-reviewed validation: fingertip PPG vs 12-lead ECG r=.997, RMSE 1.03 bpm at rest (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5368348/); HRV agreement is weaker but usable for trends — SDNN r≈0.76, RMSSD r≈0.51 vs Polar chest strap, RMSSD MAPE ~17% with wide limits of agreement, and LF/HF explicitly not trustworthy (https://academic.oup.com/europace/article/26/4/euae065/7648812, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12819663/). Note 1.4.1's first sentence still applies: the team must disclose methodology and cite that literature, and must frame it as a relative trend, not an absolute clinical value. Sleep STAGES do not survive: polysomnography studies of phone accelerometer/microphone apps found sleep-wake detection insufficiently reliable and that none of the tested apps could detect or score REM at all (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31674096/, https://jcsm.aasm.org/doi/10.5664/jcsm.4840). Sleep timing/duration is shippable; sleep architecture is research-only.

ECONOMICS, since the spec is India-first: I verified the auditor's cost claim and it holds — FreeStyle Libre sensors retail ₹4,200–₹5,249 per 14 days (https://www.flipkart.com/freestyle-libre-sensor-flash-glucose-monitoring-system-glucometer/p/itm4b0460bf79bf1, https://www.colmed.in/freestyle-libre-sensor.html). That is roughly ₹9,000–11,000/month, recurring, forever. Anchoring a core loop to it excludes essentially the entire target user base.

CONCLUSION: the ruling stands, but with a sharper boundary than the original. CGM and BP cuff are NEEDS-EXTERNAL-DEVICE *and* PLATFORM-BLOCKED for any phone-only substitute (Apple 1.4.1). Sleep staging is NEEDS-EXTERNAL-DEVICE with a research-only phone substitute. HR/HRV is the one metric that is genuinely rescuable phone-only and should be promoted out of this chapter into the core sensing tier. Device sync as a whole must be demoted from "spec feature" to "optional enrichment that no user journey, no personalization model input, and no demo script depends on."
result.workaround:
Three-tier restructure, all phone-only and all within policy.

TIER 1 (core, zero hardware, works for 100% of users): (a) Camera+flash contact PPG for resting HR and HRV, taken as a deliberate 60-second morning ritual rather than passive background sampling — validated in peer-reviewed literature, already shipping in HRV4Training/Welltory, not on Apple's 1.4.1 prohibited list. Present it as a personal baseline trend ("your HRV is 12% below your own 14-day average"), never an absolute or comparative-to-population number, and disclose the method in-app per 1.4.1's first sentence. (b) Sleep TIMING and duration from phone-idle/screen-off plus optional accelerometer, presented as time-in-bed — explicitly no stage breakdown, no REM/deep charts. (c) Symptom, cycle, mood, and food logging, which for PMOS carries more signal than any consumer sensor anyway.

TIER 2 (the honest replacement for CGM, and the one that actually fits Indian clinical reality): structured manual entry of the labs PMOS/PCOS patients are already routinely prescribed — fasting glucose + fasting insulin (auto-computing HOMA-IR), HbA1c, OGTT, lipid panel, testosterone, AMH, TSH. HOMA-IR runs about ₹1,300 in Indian metros with home collection (https://www.metropolisindia.com/parameter/homa-index-insulin-resistance-test), quarterly — roughly one-tenth the annualized cost of a Libre subscription, and it is the measurement clinicians actually act on. Add OCR-assisted capture from a photo of the lab PDF to kill the typing friction. Pair it with subjective post-meal energy/crash logging to give the n-of-1 engine a glycemic-response proxy that requires no sensor and makes no glucose claim. Critically: do NOT compute or display a predicted glucose value from food logs — that reads as "measuring blood glucose" and invites the 1.4.1 rejection through the back door.

TIER 3 (optional enrichment, clearly labelled, nothing depends on it): if the user already owns a wearable or CGM, offer import via HealthKit on iOS and Health Connect on Android, and optionally one aggregator (Terra/ROOK) for cloud-connected Fitbit/Garmin/Oura/Dexcom. Build this last. Gate it behind a settings screen, never a required onboarding step. The app must be fully functional and demoable with the toggle off, and the personalization model must degrade gracefully rather than treating device data as a required feature column — otherwise you ship two products with two accuracy profiles and can only validate one.

What the user actually accepts: the ritual-based morning HRV reading is the key trade. It is 60 seconds of finger-on-camera instead of passive wrist sensing, but it costs nothing, works on a ₹10,000 Android phone, and adherence data from HRV4Training's own user base shows people will do a daily morning measurement when it is tied to a single actionable output. Lead the demo with that plus the lab-entry insulin-resistance view, and the missing CGM never becomes the story.

result.claimOrFeature: PWA fallback for the same passive rPPG (camera-based heart rate) capture — i.e. a web/PWA path that opportunistically captures facial video for rPPG without an explicit user-initiated measurement session
result.reasoning:
UPHELD, but for tighter reasons than the auditor gave — and with two of their sub-arguments refuted.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY BLOCKED (the "passive" half — no route exists):

1. Spec-level, not just implementation-level. The mediacapture-main getUserMedia() algorithm requires the responsible document to be "fully active" and to "have focus" before capture proceeds; if not fully active it rejects with InvalidStateError, and the UA may reject outright if focus does not materialise "for an unreasonable time" (w3c/mediacapture-main issues #752 and #763 track exactly this "foreground detection" behaviour). Passive means "capture while the user is not in your page." The spec forbids the entry condition.

2. No background execution surface exists to host it. getUserMedia is unavailable in ServiceWorkerGlobalScope — the documented pattern is postMessage back to a visible window client, which defeats the purpose. And on iOS there is no background wake-up at all: Background Sync, Periodic Background Sync and Background Fetch are unimplemented in every Safari version through iOS 26.5, with no WebKit position and no experimental flag.

3. Live tracks are torn down on exactly the transitions passive sensing depends on. Chrome for Android intentionally fires mute on the video track when the screen turns off. WebKit binds the media environment to the top frame document's URL and pauses the capture session when it changes — this fires even on same-document pushState navigations (Apple Developer Forums thread 750254, WebKit PR 24971), so a PWA loses the camera on ordinary in-app routing, let alone backgrounding.

4. The unlock trigger has no web equivalent. This is the decisive one and the auditor understated it. Google's PHRM — the thing the spec is imitating — is NOT continuous background sensing. It captures an 8-second facial video "upon a screen unlock event," only within 10 minutes of unlock, only while a face is visible, and stops immediately on lock or face loss. There is no Web API that exposes device unlock. So the web cannot reproduce PHRM's trigger even in principle, and there is no substitute event with comparable semantics.

WHERE THE AUDITOR IS WRONG (does not change the verdict, but matters for the roadmap):

(a) "The PWA route forces the frames somewhere / on-device WASM rPPG is materially worse / cloud transfer creates a DPDP face-biometrics problem." This is refuted by a shipping commercial product. Binah.ai ships a Web SDK supported on mobile Safari and Chrome where "the entire process runs on the end-user's device," no internet connection required for measurement, reporting HR at ~10s and HRV / respiration / SpO2 / stress at 35-60s. Open-source on-device precedent exists too (prouast/heartbeat-js). In-browser, on-device rPPG is a solved commercial problem — the DPDP transfer risk is self-inflicted, not inherent to the web, and should not be used to justify a native-only architecture.

(b) The user-gesture / per-origin permission prompt argument is real but is the least important of the blockers. It costs one tap per session; it is not what kills passive.

THE PREMISE ITSELF NEEDS FLAGGING: "the same passive capture" presumes the native app has passive capture to fall back from. PHRM's own numbers are the ceiling, and they came with Google-scale resources: 43.1% measurement success rate in free-living use, and a severe skin-tone gap (58% light tones vs 25% dark tones) that is disqualifying for an India-first product. On iOS a third-party app has no unlock broadcast and no background camera at all. So the native "passive" tier is likely degraded-to-research-only in its own right; auditing the PWA as a "fallback" for it may be auditing a fallback for something that does not exist.
result.workaround:
A foreground, user-initiated, fully on-device "check-in" measurement in the installed PWA — deliberately NOT called passive anywhere in the spec, roadmap, or pitch.

Concretely, all phone-only and all within platform policy:
1. 30-60s facial rPPG session in an installed PWA, one tap to start, inference in WASM on-device so zero frames leave the phone. Precedent: Binah's Web SDK does exactly this shape on mobile Safari and Chrome with no internet dependency. This is DPDP-clean by construction — no biometric transfer, so no cross-border or processor questions.
2. Hold the screen with the Screen Wake Lock API for the session duration. Supported in Chrome/Edge 84+, Firefox 126+, Samsung Internet 14+, Safari 16.4+, and the long-standing bug that broke it inside installed iOS PWAs was fixed in iOS 18.4.
3. Get the ambient feel back through cadence, not sensing: a daily Web Push nudge (installed PWAs on iOS 16.4+; Declarative Web Push from 18.4) at a consistent time, so the user experiences a habit rather than a chore. This recovers most of the product intent — a longitudinal daily HR/HRV trend — without any background capture.
4. Guard the routing bug: keep the measurement screen on a single document with no pushState path changes while a track is live, or WebKit will pause the capture session mid-measurement. Also handle the visibilitychange/mute path by aborting and re-prompting rather than silently producing a bad reading.
5. Do not promise absolute values. Ship trend-over-time and a per-user baseline (n-of-1 delta framing), with an explicit quality gate that discards low-SNR sessions and tells the user to retry. Validate the skin-tone gap on your own India-first cohort before shipping any number — PHRM's 25% success on darker skin tones is the warning, not an edge case.

GREY ZONE, flag do not adopt silently: a fingertip-on-rear-camera contact PPG variant is more robust than facial rPPG on low-end Android, but it depends on torch control from the web, which I could not verify for iOS Safari (Chromium exposes torch via applyConstraints/ImageCapture; WebKit support is the open question). Treat as unverified until tested on real iOS hardware, and do not put it on a roadmap as a cross-platform path.

WHAT NOT TO DO: do not try to rescue passive by wrapping the PWA in a Trusted Web Activity or WebView shell. That makes it a native Android app subject to Play foreground-service-type declaration and the always-visible camera indicator, it does nothing for iOS, and it is no longer the PWA fallback the spec claims.

result.claimOrFeature: 'Inspired by Google's PHRM' — implying a small third-party team can replicate passive heart-rate monitoring during everyday phone use
result.reasoning:
I tried hard to refute this and failed on every path. The ruling stands, and the primary source is more damning than the auditor realized.

1. THE TRIGGER IS OS-PRIVILEGED — CONFIRMED FROM THE PAPER ITSELF, NOT JUST THE BLOG. The arXiv v3 states the system "was designed to run passively in the background and automatically initiate video capture via the front-facing camera upon a screen unlock event" (https://arxiv.org/html/2503.03783v3). That single sentence describes two capabilities a third-party app does not have on either platform:

- ANDROID: "On Android 9 (API level 28) and later, apps running in the background cannot access the camera" (https://developer.android.com/about/versions/pie/android-9.0-changes-all). The foreground-service escape hatch is explicitly closed: "if an app wants to launch a foreground service that needs while-in-use permissions (for example, body sensor, camera, microphone, or location permissions), it cannot create the service while the app is in the background, even if the app falls into one of the exemptions from background start restrictions," and on Android 14+ "if your app is in the background, and it tries to create a foreground service of type camera... the system sees that your app doesn't currently have the required permissions, and it throws a SecurityException" (https://developer.android.com/develop/background-work/services/fgs/restrictions-bg-start). So even if the team catches ACTION_USER_PRESENT, the very next line of code throws. There is no configuration of a normal Play-distributed app that reaches the camera from a background unlock event.
- iOS: there is no public unlock-event API at all, and backgrounding kills capture — AVCaptureSession.InterruptionReason.videoDeviceNotAvailableInBackground (https://developer.apple.com/documentation/AVFoundation/AVCaptureSession/InterruptionReason/videoDeviceNotAvailableInBackground). Multitasking camera access is gated behind VoIP background mode or the com.apple.developer.avfoundation.multitasking-camera-access entitlement, which must be requested from Apple and is not granted for silent health capture. A PWA is strictly worse: getUserMedia requires a visible, foregrounded, user-gestured page.

2. THE MODEL AND DATA ARE NOT LICENSABLE. Google's blog says the release is restricted to "qualified researchers" with "Institutional Review Board approval," and the dataset is "restricted entirely to non-commercial research use" (https://research.google/blog/towards-passive-heart-health-monitoring-via-smartphone-camera/). The paper adds "the informed consent agreements do not allow for sharing of participant-level data" and releases only "a pseudocode implementation." A commercial consumer app cannot build on PHRM-mini. So the team cannot even inherit the accuracy — they would have to retrain from scratch on data they do not have.

3. THE RESEARCH SETUP IS NOT REPRODUCIBLE BY 4 PEOPLE. Development used 225,773 videos from 495 participants, validation 185,970 videos from 205 participants, across 26 phone models, with clips at 640x480/15fps and participants manually reviewing and authorizing every video upload. The authors state "we did not account for constraints on battery consumption in favor of collecting more data" — i.e. the passive capture loop was never engineered to be shippable. Limitations include degraded success rates on the darkest skin tones and high error with "frequent head motion and talking," which is precisely what everyday unlock conditions look like.

4. CORRECTION TO THE AUDITOR'S OWN EVIDENCE (this matters, and reinforces the verdict). The auditor cited "192k training videos, 485 participants" and "face authentication." The published v3 says 225,773 videos / 495 participants for development (~412k videos, ~700 participants total per the blog's rounding), and the trigger is a SCREEN unlock event, not specifically face authentication. The auditor's numbers are from a stale preprint version. This does not rescue the feature — it makes the citation problem worse, because the spec is anchoring investor-facing claims to a moving research target whose numbers the team is already reporting incorrectly.

5. WHAT ACTUALLY SHIPS TODAY, AND WHY IT ISN'T THIS. Real third-party camera-PPG products exist — Binah.ai ships a commercial iOS/Android rPPG SDK (https://www.binah.ai/sdk/), Lifelight has Class II certification, and Google Fit ships camera heart rate on both Android and iOS (https://support.google.com/fit/answer/10477667). Every one of them is USER-INITIATED and FOREGROUND: hold still / put your finger on the lens for 30-60 seconds. None is passive. The gap between "shipping product" and "PHRM" is exactly the OS hook, and that gap is not closable with effort or money.

CONCLUSION: the sentence "inspired by Google's PHRM" is not a factual error about rPPG — rPPG works. It is a false implication of transferability. It will read to a judge or investor as "proven, we just implement it," when the one component that makes PHRM passive is the one component a third party can never obtain. Delete the framing or rewrite it to state the limitation in the same breath.
result.workaround: Replace "passive HR sensing" with an honest two-layer design. LAYER 1 (the real passive layer, genuinely phone-only and shippable today): behavioural and motion signals the OS already grants without the camera — step count and activity from Core Motion / Android motion sensors (built into the phone, no external device), screen-time and unlock-frequency rhythm, typing-time-of-day as a sleep-window proxy, and in-app logging cadence. This carries the "passive sensing" narrative truthfully and is where the n-of-1 personalization engine should actually feed from. LAYER 2 (the HR measurement, honest about being active): a user-initiated 30-60s CONTACT PPG "pulse check" — fingertip on the rear camera with the torch on, foreground, with a visible countdown. Contact PPG measurably outperforms non-contact face rPPG in consumer conditions (Coppetti et al., Eur J Prev Cardiol 2017: contact-PPG apps had "higher feasibility and better accuracy" than non-contact — https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/2047487317702044), it works in poor lighting, and it degrades gracefully on darker skin tones where face rPPG does not. Prompt it opportunistically at natural moments the user is already in the app (morning check-in, cycle log, post-symptom entry) to accumulate a resting-HR TREND over weeks — which delivers most of PHRM's actual product value (trend, not spot value) without any OS hook. Ship it as an optional module: if a user misses days, the trend degrades, it does not break. Do NOT call this passive anywhere in the spec, deck, or UI. Two hard guardrails: (a) Apple guideline 1.4.1 permits camera heart rate — Google Fit and Instant Heart Rate ship on iOS — but explicitly bans device-sensor-only blood pressure, blood glucose, blood oxygen and temperature ("apps that claim to take x-rays, measure blood pressure, body temperature, blood glucose levels, or blood oxygen levels using only the sensors on the device are not permitted," https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/), so the camera path must never be extended to BP or glucose regardless of what any vendor SDK offers; (b) if the team licenses a commercial SDK (e.g. Binah) rather than training their own, budget for per-measurement licensing and note that this is a vendor dependency, not owned IP. If PHRM must be cited at all, cite it only as directional evidence that camera rPPG can approach wearable-grade resting HR, with the sentence "the passive trigger PHRM uses is an OS-level unlock hook unavailable to third-party apps; our equivalent is user-initiated" in the same paragraph.
