You can only get USER_PRESENT via a runtime-registered receiver, which requires a live process, which for a well-being app means already running a persistent foreground service with a permanent notification. So the "silent trigger" premise fails on its own terms.

2) THE FGS BACKGROUND-START EXEMPTION LIST DOES NOT RESCUE IT. There are 14 documented exemptions from FGS background-start restrictions (high-priority FCM, exact alarm, battery-optimization disabled, SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW, geofence transition, BOOT_COMPLETED, etc. — https://developer.android.com/develop/background-work/services/fgs/restrictions-bg-start). I checked each. None of them help, because camera is gated by a SECOND, independent rule: "If your app is in the background and it tries to create a foreground service of type camera, location, or microphone, the system sees that your app doesn't currently have the required permissions, and it throws a SecurityException." The exemption list for THAT rule is a completely separate, much shorter list.

3) THE WHILE-IN-USE EXEMPTION LIST IS ENTIRELY USER-INITIATED OR PRIVILEGED. Verbatim from the same page, section "Exemptions from while-in-use permission restrictions": a system component starts the service; the service starts by interacting with app widgets; the service starts by interacting with a notification; the service starts as a PendingIntent sent from a different, visible app; the service is started by a device policy controller in device owner mode; started by an app providing VoiceInteractionService; started by an app with the privileged START_ACTIVITIES_FROM_BACKGROUND permission. Note what is conspicuously ABSENT: SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW/overlay, disabled battery optimization, and high-priority FCM — the three exemptions people usually reach for — are background-start exemptions only and do NOT confer while-in-use camera access. The three that a consumer app could theoretically reach (widget tap, notification tap, PendingIntent from another visible app) all require an explicit user tap, which by definition makes the capture active, not passive. Device-owner DPC is enterprise-provisioned (not a Play consumer install), and VoiceInteractionService requires the user to make a PMOS app their device's default assistant — technically reachable but absurd as product design and certain to draw Play review scrutiny. The privileged permission is a system-image-only grant. This is Google-and-OEM-only territory, exactly the OS-vendor privilege distinction the audit context flags.

4) EVEN IF YOU GOT THERE, PLAY POLICY AND THE PRIVACY INDICATOR KILL "PASSIVE". The only approved Play use case for the camera FGS type is "Continue to access the camera from the background. For example, video chat apps that allow for multitasking" (https://developer.android.com/develop/background-work/services/fgs/service-types). Play Console requires a written justification, user-impact statement, and a demo video proving user-initiated, user-perceptible use for each declared FGS type (https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/13392821). "Silently photograph the user's face at unlock" is not that use case and would not survive the declaration review. Separately, since Android 12 the green camera privacy indicator fires on every camera open and cannot be suppressed by any app (https://source.android.com/docs/core/permissions/privacy-indicators) — so even a legally-started background camera FGS is announced by a green dot plus a permanent notification. Unobtrusive passive facial capture is not merely blocked by permissions; it is architecturally impossible to hide by OS design.

5) NO SHIPPING APP DOES THIS. The state of the art in phone-only camera vitals — NuraLogix Anura (https://anura.ai/faq/) and Binah.ai (https://www.binah.ai/) — are all explicitly active-session: the user holds the phone up, frames their face, and holds still for 7-45 seconds with a visible activity in the foreground. If passive background capture were reachable, the best-funded rPPG vendors in the category would already be shipping it. They are not.

THE ONE THING THAT IS LEGAL, and worth stating precisely so it isn't confused with a refutation: a camera FGS started while an activity is visible retains camera access after the user leaves the app. That is real. But it does not produce the spec's feature — it requires the session to have begun with the user inside the app, it carries a permanent notification and green dot, and it burns battery holding the camera pipeline open for a signal that is worthless when the phone is face-down or in a pocket, which is the overwhelming majority of the time. Secondary and unverified (search budget exhausted before I could cite it): India-first distribution makes this worse, since aggressive OEM process-killing on MIUI/HyperOS, ColorOS and Funtouch routinely terminates long-lived foreground services, so even the legal version would be unreliable on the target market's dominant handsets.

Verdict: the auditor's reasoning is correct and, if anything, understated — the feature is blocked at three independent layers (broadcast delivery, while-in-use permission model, Play FGS policy) plus an un-suppressible OS privacy indicator. This must not enter the roadmap or any investor/judge-facing deck as a capability.

Reframe from "passive capture" to "zero-extra-effort in-session capture", which needs no FGS at all and is fully compliant. Three layers, in priority order:

1. IN-SESSION AMBIENT rPPG (primary; genuinely shippable). Run the front camera only while the user has a visible activity open — during the 30-60s they already spend reading their daily insight card or logging symptoms. No foreground service, no background-start rule, no Play FGS declaration; the app is simply in the foreground, which is where camera access is unconditionally legal. From the user's point of view this is passive: they do nothing extra, they just use the app. Requires prominent in-app disclosure and consent per Play's personal/sensitive data policy, plus a visible on-screen "camera active" affordance so the green dot is never a surprise. Ship the output as a low-confidence directional trend (a wellness signal), never as a vital sign — uncontrolled lighting, distance, motion and skin tone all degrade face rPPG badly, and a 4-person team cannot clinically validate it.

2. UNLOCK-TRIGGERED PROMPT, NOT UNLOCK-TRIGGERED CAPTURE. Keep the unlock/context intent, but move the camera behind the documented notification-interaction exemption: post a contextual check-in notification, and when the user taps it, the camera FGS (or plain activity) starts legally with while-in-use access. This is the closest sanctioned analogue to the spec's intent and is explicitly listed in Android's while-in-use exemptions. Cost: one tap. Benefit: it ships.

3. BETTER SIGNAL, SAME ZERO HARDWARE — REAR-CAMERA FINGERTIP PPG. If the actual product need is HR/HRV rather than face imaging, contact PPG (fingertip on the rear lens with the flash on, 60-90s, user-initiated) has a dramatically better signal-to-noise ratio than face rPPG and is the technique behind the most credible phone-only heart-rate features. Fully foreground, fully phone-only, no purchased device, no platform conflict.

What NOT to do: do not attempt SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW overlays, disabled battery optimization, high-priority FCM wakeups, accessibility services, or a default-assistant VoiceInteractionService as a route to background camera. The first three are documented as NOT conferring while-in-use camera access; the last two are either irrelevant to camera permission or a product-destroying misuse of a system role. Any of them presented to Play review reads as covert camera access and risks removal of the whole app.

Access gate is a Google Form requiring a verified academic email, IRB-approved protocol, and an encryption/security plan. The auditor's double-bar point is correct and is actually sharper than stated: "non-clinical" bars the health framing even for a hypothetical non-profit version of this app.

2) NEW — THERE IS NO "LET GOOGLE COMPUTE IT" BACKDOOR. My strongest refutation candidate was that the team need not license the model at all if Google shipped PHRM in a consumer app (Fitbit/Google Fit/Pixel) that writes heart rate to Health Connect, which any third-party app can read with user consent. That would have been phone-only, device-free, license-clean, and genuinely shippable. It does not exist. The Google Research blog confirms PHRM is a research system that has NOT shipped in any Google consumer product; what was released was the dataset and the pre-trained model, to qualified academic researchers only. There is no product surface producing PHRM-derived heart rate for anyone to read. Refutation dead.

3) NEW — EVEN A CLEAN-ROOM REIMPLEMENTATION CANNOT SHIP THE *PASSIVE* PART. Suppose the team ignores the weights and reimplements from the published paper. The defining mechanism of PHRM is automatic 8-second front-camera video capture triggered on every screen-unlock event. Both platforms forbid exactly that for third-party apps. iOS suspends camera access when an app backgrounds; the only override is the com.apple.developer.avfoundation.multitasking-camera-access entitlement, which Apple grants for VoIP multitasking, not for opportunistic health capture. Android's `camera` foreground-service type is explicitly subject to while-in-use restrictions — the docs state you "cannot create a camera foreground service while your app is in the background and you cannot launch a camera foreground service from a BOOT_COMPLETED receiver." So the passive capture loop is platform-blocked independently of any licensing question. This is the OS-vendor-privilege asymmetry the build context warns about: Google could do this in its own first-party app; a 4-person third party cannot.

4) NEW — NO COMMERCIALLY-LICENSED TRAINING DATA, AND THE BUILD ITSELF WOULD NEED BANNED HARDWARE. Training a substitute model needs labelled video. rPPG-Toolbox's *code* is under the Responsible AI Source Code License v1.1, which does grant commercial rights — the one genuinely permissive thing I found — but its pretrained weights derive from UBFC-rPPG, PURE, MMPD and similar academic datasets whose own terms do not convey commercial rights, so the weights do not inherit the toolbox's commercial grant. Collecting proprietary data instead requires simultaneous ground-truth HR from ECG or a wearable — a build-time external-hardware dependency (grey zone: it is not shipped to users, but it is a real capex and headcount the spec never budgets). Scale reference: Google used 225,773 videos from 495 participants across six prospective studies. Not a 4-person-team artefact.

5) THE FEATURE IS A BAD BET EVEN IF ALL OF THE ABOVE WERE FREE — AND THIS IS THE PART THE ROADMAP SHOULD ACTUALLY FEAR. PHRM's own paper reports a free-living measurement success rate of 43.1%, stratified by skin tone at 58% light / 45% medium / 25% dark. For an India-first product, a passive HR feature that silently fails for roughly three-quarters of darker-skinned users is a fairness failure and a support nightmare, not a headline feature. Google's 4.58 bpm MAE was achieved *on the successful 43%*. Anyone demoing "passive heart rate" to judges on this basis is promising something that will not survive contact with the target market.

WHY I AM KEEPING THE LABEL "RESEARCH-ONLY" RATHER THAN "PLATFORM-BLOCKED": the claim as written is about *using Google's released artefacts*, and those are literally licensed research-only. The platform block is a second, independent barrier that applies to the reimplementation fallback. Flagging both matters, because a team told only "the license blocks you" will predictably respond "fine, we'll train our own" and burn months hitting barrier 3.
result.workaround:
USER-INITIATED CONTACT PPG — finger on the rear camera with the torch on. This is genuinely shippable today by a 4-person team, phone-only, no license, no external device.

WHY IT CLEARS EVERY GATE. (a) No model, no dataset, no license: it is classical signal processing — bandpass the red-channel mean over a 60-90s window and do peak/interval detection. Decades-old public technique, nothing to license from anyone. (b) Accuracy is real and citable: the JMIR validation study found fingertip smartphone PPG vs ECG at r=.997, RMSE 1.03 bpm at rest, and notably found fingertip agreement *better* than facial/rPPG — i.e. the contact method is more accurate than the passive one you are giving up. (c) Time-domain HRV is supported: published work shows good agreement with ECG for NN, SDNN and RMSSD. (d) Store-legal: Apple's Guideline 1.4.1 enumerates the banned device-sensor-only measurements as "x-rays, blood pressure, body temperature, blood glucose levels, or blood oxygen levels" — heart rate is conspicuously absent from that list, and commercial contact-PPG apps (Instant Heart Rate, Welltory, HRV4Training) ship on both stores. The guideline's other half still binds you: "Apps must clearly disclose data and methodology to support accuracy claims" — so publish your method and cite the validation literature in-app.

HOW TO MAKE IT A FEATURE RATHER THAN A DOWNGRADE, FOR PMOS SPECIFICALLY. Ship it as a 60-second morning check-in ritual, not a measurement chore. Track resting HR and RMSSD as a rolling personal baseline with deviation bands — this is n-of-1 personalization done honestly, since the user is their own control and you never need population-normal ranges. For PMOS this is arguably better aligned than passive HR anyway: the clinically interesting axis is autonomic tone and stress load over weeks, which a consistent same-time-each-day measurement captures more cleanly than opportunistic unlock-triggered snapshots taken at random arousal states. The daily ritual also gives you the retention loop and the symptom-logging hook that a silent background sensor never would.

THE HONEST COST: you trade zero-effort passivity for daily compliance. Say that plainly in the spec. Expect 40-60% daily adherence and design the insights to degrade gracefully on gaps — which, note, is roughly the same coverage PHRM's passive approach actually achieved in free-living conditions, so you are giving up less than the spec implies.

HARD LINES — DO NOT CROSS. Do not claim blood pressure, blood glucose, SpO2, or temperature from the camera: those are named in 1.4.1 and will get the app rejected outright, and a glucose claim in a PMOS app is exactly the pitch a judge or investor will probe. Do not present HRV as predicting or diagnosing cycle phase, ovulation, or insulin resistance — keep it observational trend data with an explicit non-diagnostic disclaimer. Do not describe any of this as "passive" in marketing; it is user-initiated, and the word invites the comparison to Google that you will lose. Do not cite PHRM's 4.58 bpm MAE as your expected accuracy — cite the contact-PPG literature you are actually implementing.

FINDING 1 — the PHRM artifact is legally off-limits, not merely immature. Google released a dataset plus a "PHRM-mini" pre-trained model, and both are gated. The blog states the dataset is "restricted entirely to non-commercial research use" and that "qualified researchers can apply for access." The repo terms require a verified academic email, an IRB-approved study protocol, a security plan, and written consent not to share with third parties, and forbid use "for any purpose other than non-commercial, non-clinical research purposes." There is no open-weights drop, no permissive license, no download without an application. A 4-person commercial consumer app is excluded by the license itself. This is the strongest possible form of "research-only": enforced by contract, not by model quality.
Sources: https://research.google/blog/towards-passive-heart-health-monitoring-via-smartphone-camera/ ; https://github.com/Google-Health/consumer-health-research/tree/main/rppg

FINDING 2 — it did not land in any Google developer surface. HAI-DEF, Google's open-weight health model program, ships MedGemma, MedASR, MedSigLIP, TxGemma, HeAR, and Path Foundation. There is no rPPG, PPG, heart-rate, or camera-based physiological model in the catalogue. The auditor's ML Kit enumeration is also correct — no vitals API. Health Connect's HeartRateRecord/RestingHeartRateRecord are storage schemas on a local data bus that aggregates from Wear OS, Samsung Health, Fitbit and Garmin; it will store a bpm you computed but will never produce one from a camera.
Sources: https://developers.google.com/health-ai-developer-foundations ; https://developers.google.com/ml-kit ; https://developer.android.com/health-and-fitness/health-services/health-platform

That framing is misleading here, because even a perfect, freely-licensed rPPG model does not give a third party PHRM. PHRM's entire product value is that it is PASSIVE — it captures front-camera frames in the seconds after face-unlock events, with no user session. A third-party app cannot do that on either OS:
- Android: "If your app starts a foreground service while running in the background, the foreground service cannot access the microphone or camera." Camera access is while-in-use only. (https://developer.android.com/about/versions/11/privacy/foreground-services ; https://developer.android.com/develop/background-work/services/fgs/service-types)
- iOS: backgrounding an app interrupts the capture session with reason videoDeviceNotAvailableInBackground. The escape hatch, isMultitaskingCameraAccessSupported, is true only for apps declaring the voip background mode or holding the com.apple.developer.avfoundation.multitasking-camera-access entitlement, which must be requested from and granted by Apple and is scoped to video-conferencing. A PMOS wellness app will not get it. (https://developer.apple.com/documentation/AVFoundation/AVCaptureSession/InterruptionReason/videoDeviceNotAvailableInBackground)
- Neither OS exposes a face-unlock event hook to third parties at all.
Google shipped PHRM as research because Google is the OS vendor and can hook the biometric unlock path. That privilege is not licensable. This is a permanent structural block, not a timing problem.

FINDING 4 — the one real refutation I found, and why it does not save the pillar. Commercial camera-vitals SDKs genuinely exist and are licensable by a small team: Binah.ai (white-label SDK, iOS 15+/Android 10+, explicitly App Store and Play compatible, HR/HRV/SpO2/respiration/stress, per-session or per-user pricing) and FaceHeart FH Vitals (FDA-cleared Class II SaMD for HR and respiration rate). So "no third party can ever get bpm from a phone camera" would be wrong. But neither is passive: both are ~60-second active spot checks with the user holding still in front of the app. They refute "no camera-vitals SDK exists"; they do not refute "PHRM is available to us." And FaceHeart's SaMD clearance drags the product toward the regulated-device status the spec explicitly wants to avoid, while Binah's per-session pricing is a poor fit for a free-tier India-first consumer app at scale.
Sources: https://www.binah.ai/sdk/ ; https://faceheart.com/sdk.php ; https://veyetals.com/integrate/

BOTTOM LINE FOR THE ROADMAP: delete every occurrence of the words "PHRM," "passive," and "background" from this pillar. Any spec language implying the app senses heart rate while the user goes about their day is unbuildable by this team and should not be shown to judges or investors. Cite the Nature paper as inspiration if you like, but the implementation must be an active, foreground, user-initiated measurement.

POLICY NOTE the parent should carry forward: whichever active path is chosen, Google Play's Health apps declaration applies, and from January 2026 Play adds Medical Device labelling plus stricter justification for health data reads. Keep the framing strictly non-diagnostic wellness, ship a visible "not a medical device, do not use for diagnosis" disclaimer, and never surface a number next to a clinical threshold. (https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/13996367 ; https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/16679511)

SHIPPABLE REPLACEMENT: a user-initiated 30-60 second CONTACT PPG "daily pulse check" using the rear camera plus torch, with the fingertip over the lens. This is fully phone-only, needs no purchased device, no OS privilege, no gated model, and no licensed SDK.

Why contact and not face-based rPPG: contact fingertip PPG is the method with the strongest independent validation. Peer-reviewed comparisons put smartphone contact-PPG within roughly 1-5 bpm of ECG/Polar reference at rest, and the Azumio Instant Heart Rate app using exactly this method has shipped on the App Store and Play for over a decade at very large scale, which is your regulatory and review-process precedent. Build shape for a 4-person team: torch-on + rear camera preview, extract per-frame mean red-channel intensity from a centre ROI, bandpass 0.7-3.5 Hz, peak-detect or FFT for the dominant frequency, require ~30s of stable signal, and hard-fail with "we couldn't get a clean reading, try again" rather than emitting a low-confidence number. Ship a confidence gate and never display a bpm you do not trust. This is a well-trodden signal-processing problem with abundant open-source reference implementations; it is a two-to-three week build, not a research project.

Product framing that makes ACTIVE acceptable to the user: PMOS users already have a daily morning ritual (temperature, symptoms, mood logging). Fold a 60-second "morning resting HR" into that ritual as one more step, done once a day before getting out of bed, which is also the physiologically correct time for resting HR. You get the same downstream signal PHRM was going to provide — a per-user resting-HR baseline and deviation trend for the n-of-1 engine — at roughly one reading per day instead of many. Streaks and a visible trend line carry the adherence. Be honest in the spec that this trades passive coverage for user effort, and budget for real adherence decay.

Plumbing: write the computed value to Health Connect (HeartRateRecord / RestingHeartRateRecord) on Android and HealthKit on iOS so it lives alongside the user's other data and survives app churn. This is the correct and intended use of Health Connect as a data bus, and it does not contradict the auditor's point.

GREY ZONE, flag explicitly, do not make it core: if a user already owns a watch or ring, let them opt into importing heart rate from Health Connect or HealthKit. This is a legitimate enhancement and costs almost nothing to build once the write path exists. But it must be strictly additive — no screen, insight, or onboarding step may assume it, and it must never be shown to judges as the mechanism, or the no-external-devices constraint has been violated by the back door.

result.claimOrFeature: Passive front-camera rPPG capture on iOS while the app is backgrounded or immediately on unlock (Google PHRM-style), built by a 4-person third-party team, phone-only.
result.reasoning:
VERDICT UPHELD — BUT THE AUDITOR'S STATED REASONING IS PARTLY WRONG AND MUST BE CORRECTED BEFORE THIS AUDIT IS SHOWN TO ANYONE TECHNICAL.

=== WHERE THE AUDITOR IS FACTUALLY WRONG ===

The auditor asserts "iOS has no camera background mode." As of iOS 18 that is false, and a reviewer who knows this will discard the entire audit. Apple's own documentation for AVCaptureSession.isMultitaskingCameraAccessSupported states the property is true when: "The app runs on an iPad that supports Stage Manager with an extended display. / The app links against iOS 18 or later and uses `voip` as one of its UIBackgroundModes. / The app has the com.apple.developer.avfoundation.multitasking-camera-access entitlement." (https://developer.apple.com/documentation/avfoundation/avcapturesession/ismultitaskingcameraaccesssupported). Setting isMultitaskingCameraAccessEnabled = true on such a session keeps the camera delivering frames while the app is backgrounded. Third-party SDK documentation confirms the practical behavior: by default "iOS will disable the camera" on backgrounding, but the camera remains available with the VoIP background mode or the entitlement (https://getstream.io/video/docs/ios/advanced/background-modes/). So a background camera path genuinely exists for third-party apps. The auditor's videoDeviceNotAvailableInBackground citation describes only the DEFAULT case.

=== WHY THE BLOCK SURVIVES ANYWAY (five independent reasons, any one fatal) ===

1. POLICY ELIGIBILITY. The gate is being a VoIP/video-conferencing app. Declaring `voip` in UIBackgroundModes in a PMOS wellness companion that places no calls is a direct violation of App Store Review Guideline 2.5.4: "Multitasking apps may only use background services for their intended purposes: VoIP, audio playback, location, task completion, local notifications, etc." (https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/). Declared background modes are inspected against actual functionality at review. This converts a technical opening into a hard policy block, which is worse — there is no engineering workaround for a guideline. The alternative route, com.apple.developer.avfoundation.multitasking-camera-access, is a request-only entitlement granted for conferencing; a 4-person startup will not receive it to silently film users' faces.

2. IT IS NOT PASSIVE EVEN IF GRANTED. Multitasking camera access only preserves a session that is ALREADY RUNNING. The user must open the app and start the camera in the foreground first. There is no spontaneous, unattended start. "Passive sensing" is unachievable regardless of entitlement — the best case is "user starts a measurement, then leaves the app and it continues."

3. THE ON-UNLOCK TRIGGER DOES NOT EXIST AT ALL. This half of the claim is unrescuable. There is no public API for screen lock/unlock state; the notify_keys.h notifications developers reach for are private API and grounds for rejection (https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/69333). BGTaskScheduler is opportunistic and system-scheduled, gives no delivery guarantee, does not run until first unlock after reboot, and confers no camera access. PHRM's "measure on unlock" is an OS-vendor privilege, full stop.

4. THE GREEN INDICATOR CANNOT BE SUPPRESSED. It persists on the Home Screen and inside every other app for the entire capture. For a reproductive-health app in an India-first market, a permanent green camera dot is a trust and press liability, not a UX nit. The auditor is right on this point.

5. NO VENDOR CLAIMS THIS, WHICH IS THE STRONGEST EVIDENCE. The state of the art in commercial camera rPPG — Binah.ai, App Store-compatible, iPhone XS and later — is a deliberate 30–60 second spot check requiring the user to sit still, not talk, and be well lit (https://www.binah.ai/sdk/, https://www.binah.ai/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/Heart-Rate-validation-report.pdf). If passive background rPPG were viable on iOS, the funded specialists would ship it. They do not. The only backgrounded state where a face is even in frame is "user is looking at the phone in another app," where off-axis pose, motion, and variable screen illumination push rPPG below usable quality. Add continuous front-camera capture plus per-frame ML inference as one of the heaviest sustained power loads available to an app — PHRM runs on privileged low-power OS paths a third party cannot touch.

BOTTOM LINE: Ship the corrected reasoning. "iOS forbids background camera" is wrong and will be caught. "iOS gates background camera behind a VoIP-app eligibility test we cannot honestly pass, the mechanism is not passive even if we passed it, the unlock trigger has no API in principle, and no rPPG vendor on earth claims background operation" is correct and unarguable. NOT downgraded to RESEARCH-ONLY, because the barrier is platform policy and a missing OS trigger, not accuracy — the accuracy problem is merely the second wall behind the first.
result.workaround:
VIABLE, PHONE-ONLY, AND ARGUABLY A BETTER PRODUCT — a deliberate foreground spot check on a daily anchor.

PRIMARY SIGNAL — rear-camera CONTACT PPG, not face rPPG. User covers the rear lens with a fingertip, torch on, 45 seconds, foreground. Signal-to-noise is far higher than facial rPPG because you have direct tissue contact and a controlled light source, it works in any ambient lighting, and Azumio/Instant Heart Rate-class apps have shipped it for over a decade. This is category (a): genuinely shippable today by a 4-person team. Front-camera face rPPG can ship as a secondary no-touch option, foreground only, with hard quality gating (face detected, adequate luminance, low motion) that REFUSES to emit a number rather than emitting a bad one.

REPLACING THE UNLOCK TRIGGER — you cannot trigger on unlock, so do not try. Use a fixed daily local notification plus a Lock Screen / Home Screen widget prompting a wake-time check-in, optionally with a Live Activity during the measurement. This is not a consolation prize: a single resting HR/HRV measurement taken on waking under consistent conditions is a CLEANER baseline for detecting luteal-phase and cycle-related trend shifts than a scatter of opportunistic samples of unknown posture, lighting, and activity state. Sampling discipline beats sampling frequency for n-of-1 trend detection.

WHAT TO PROMISE: "45 seconds each morning" — honest, achievable, no hardware, no entitlement, no guideline risk. WHAT TO DELETE FROM THE SPEC: the words "passive," "background," and "on unlock" as applied to camera capture. Requires no wearable, no CGM, no add-on hardware, so the phone-only constraint is fully satisfied.

The auditor wrote that the Screen Time stack "reports app-usage thresholds, not raw unlock events." That understates what exists. Apple's DeviceActivity framework DOES expose pickup counts through public API: DeviceActivityData.ApplicationActivity.numberOfPickups and ActivitySegment.totalPickupsWithoutApplicationActivity. "Pickups" is Apple's own unlock/wake-and-look metric — semantically the exact number the spec wants. So the claim "iOS has no unlock data anywhere" is false.

It is nonetheless unusable for this spec, for four independent reasons, any one of which is fatal:

1. SANDBOX EXFILTRATION BAN (the decisive one). Those numbers are readable only inside a DeviceActivityReportExtension, which Apple sandboxes specifically to prevent network requests and to prevent moving sensitive content outside the extension's address space. The extension can render a SwiftUI view that your app embeds, but your app process cannot read the integer, persist it, sync it, or join it against cycle/symptom data. The n-of-1 personalization engine in the spec requires exactly that join. Developers hitting this report that attempting to pass usage data to the main app "returns absolutely nothing" — by design, not by bug.

2. IT IS A REPORT, NOT A TRIGGER. Even if the number escaped, DeviceActivityReport is retrospective rendering. It cannot wake your app to start a PPG measurement. On that half of the claim Apple DTS is on the record twice, unambiguously: on unlock — "For this to work the system would have to resume (or relaunch) your app in the background every time the device is unlocked, and there's no facility to do that... The only other way... would be for the system to maintain these metrics for you, and give you access to them via some API. Again, there's no API for that." (forums/thread/751215). And on screen sleep/wake — Quinn: "There is no supported way to be notified of sleep and wake events on iOS," adding that any such mechanism would have to be a historical timeline, which does not exist (forums/thread/744375).

3. ENTITLEMENT GATE. Everything in FamilyControls/DeviceActivity requires com.apple.developer.family-controls, a privileged entitlement Apple grants case-by-case, scoped to parental-control and screen-wellbeing use. A menstrual-health companion is a speculative fit. A 4-person team cannot put a core roadmap feature behind a discretionary Apple approval with a multi-week-to-indefinite turnaround and no appeal.

4. THE KNOWN WORKAROUND IS DEAD IN CURRENT iOS. The one published trick for getting usage signal out of the sandbox (register many DeviceActivityMonitor threshold events at 5-minute increments and count callbacks) measures app foreground TIME, not pickups, and is coarse (5-10 min), capped at ~20-21 concurrent activities, and history-free. On top of that, iOS 26 shipped heavy DeviceActivity regressions — didReachThreshold firing immediately on event creation, and callbacks reported unreliable past roughly 45 minutes, unfixed for months.

Private SpringBoard notifications (com.apple.springboard.lockstate / lockcomplete) remain a documented rejection cause under the non-public-API guideline. protectedDataDidBecomeAvailableNotification is real but only fires in an already-running process — it is a file-protection signal, so it can never be an unlock counter. Both auditor points stand.

I also checked the obvious escape hatch of "skip unlock, read sleep from Health instead." It is also degraded phone-only: without a watch, HealthKit sleep from iPhone is inBed only, and Apple stopped recording inBed samples as of iOS 18 / watchOS 11; the user's configured bedtime/wake-up schedule is explicitly NOT exposed through HealthKit. So there is no honest phone-only "measured sleep" input either. Do not let the spec quietly substitute a watch here — that would violate the no-external-devices constraint.

PARTIAL RESCUE WORTH NAMING: a display-only version is shippable — embed a DeviceActivityReport view so the user can SEE their own pickup count next to their cycle phase, entitlement permitting. It is a legitimate UI feature. It is not the spec'd feature, because the app itself stays blind to the number.

No shipping third-party iOS app can be doing this differently; apps that surface "pickups" (Opal, one sec, ScreenZen class) are consistent with the render-only path above, which is why none of them let you export or correlate that number outside their own report view.
result.workaround:
Replace "unlock" with two things the user consents to explicitly. Both are 100% public API, no entitlement, phone-only, App Store safe.

(A) SLEEP/WAKE — App Intents + user-installed Shortcuts personal automations, set to Run Immediately. Apple's documented triggers include a Sleep category ("Wind Down Begins", "Bedtime Begins", "Waking Up", driven by the user's Health sleep schedule), Alarm ("Is Stopped", scoped to the Wake-up alarm), Focus ("When Turning On"/"When Turning Off"), Charger ("Is Connected"/"Is Disconnected"), and App ("Is Opened"/"Is Closed"). Ship an App Intent like "Log Sleep Marker", plus a guided 60-second onboarding that walks the user through adding 3 automations (Bedtime Begins, Waking Up, Charger Connected). Each fires your intent, which timestamps locally. This captures the user's intended sleep window plus a night-charging corroborator. Be honest in the UI that this is a schedule-and-behavior marker, not measured sleep — never call it sleep staging.

(B) MEASUREMENT TRIGGER — stop trying to trigger on unlock, which no consumer HR app does anyway. Use a scheduled local notification at a user-chosen morning slot ("30-second check-in") plus a BGAppRefreshTask to prep state, and have the user tap to run the camera PPG measurement. Tap-to-measure is the shipping norm and is what makes the reading usable at all, since PPG needs a still finger on the lens.

(C) FREE PHONE-USE SIGNAL YOU ALREADY OWN — your own app's scenePhase / willEnterForegroundNotification gives first-open-of-day, session count, and time-of-day rhythm for YOUR app, with zero entitlement. Combined with (A) this is enough to build a "morning check-in time drifted later this week" style insight. It is a proxy for the user's engagement rhythm, not for device unlocks, and must be labelled as such internally so no one later reports it as a screen-time metric.

Explicitly rejected as workarounds: any wearable or watch (violates no-external-devices), the Screen Time entitlement as a load-bearing dependency (discretionary Apple approval + sandbox still blocks the data), private SpringBoard notifications (rejection risk), and the threshold-counting hack (wrong metric, broken on iOS 26).

PWA note: none of this exists on iOS Safari at all — no Screen Time, no App Intents, no background wake. If the PWA is a shipping target, the sleep/wake feature is manual-entry-only there.

result.claimOrFeature: Spec cites Nature (June 2026) paper on Google PHRM (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10507-6) as the basis for passive, phone-only heart-rate / resting-heart-rate monitoring in the PMOS companion app.
result.reasoning:
I tried hard to refute this and could not. I could only make the auditor's ruling stronger and more precise.

WHAT I CONFIRMED ABOUT THE CITATION (auditor correct)
Liao, S., Di Achille, P., Wu, J. et al., "Passive heart-rate monitoring during smartphone use in everyday life", Nature 655, 728-736 (2026), DOI 10.1038/s41586-026-10507-6; preprint arXiv:2503.03783. Real paper, correctly attributed, Google Research. So this is NOT a fabricated-citation problem. The defect is the implied status.

ONE CORRECTION TO THE AUDITOR'S EVIDENCE (which cuts against the spec, not for it)
The auditor said code availability is "pseudocode only." That understates what exists but does not help the team: Google did release a GitHub repo with a pre-trained "PHRM-mini" model plus the rPPG video dataset — but access is explicitly gated to qualified researchers with IRB approval and NON-COMMERCIAL intent (https://research.google/blog/towards-passive-heart-health-monitoring-via-smartphone-camera/). A 4-person team shipping a consumer app on the App Store / Play Store cannot use those weights. So the one artifact that looked like a shortcut is license-blocked. Nothing to fork.

WHY THE "PASSIVE" PART IS ALSO PLATFORM-BLOCKED FOR A THIRD PARTY (independent, harder blocker)
The mechanism is not "camera measures HR" — it is unlock-triggered background facial video. Per the paper's methods: front camera, capture triggered by screen-unlock, face must be detected within 5s of unlock, 8-second clips at 15 FPS, repeating up to 30 times per unlock for up to 10 minutes of video, running while the user does whatever they were doing. That is exactly the capture pattern both platforms forbid to third-party apps:
- Android: "If your app starts a foreground service while running in the background, the foreground service cannot access the microphone or camera." (https://developer.android.com/about/versions/11/privacy/foreground-services). There is no "allow all the time" grant for CAMERA the way there is for location. An unlock broadcast handler cannot legally get a camera stream.
- iOS: camera capture is interrupted the moment the app backgrounds (AVCaptureSession.InterruptionReason.videoDeviceNotAvailableInBackground). The only escape is isMultitaskingCameraAccessSupported, which is true only for VoIP-background-mode video-conferencing apps or holders of the com.apple.developer.avfoundation.multitasking-camera-access entitlement, which must be requested from and granted by Apple (https://developer.apple.com/documentation/AVFoundation/AVCaptureSession/InterruptionReason/videoDeviceNotAvailableInBackground). A PMOS wellness app is not getting that entitlement, and even with it, iOS gives no third-party hook on Face ID unlock at all.
Google's own framing depends on privileges it has as the OS vendor: on-device processing possibly inside Android's Trusted Execution Environment, Android's face-AR landmark model, and the face-authentication event itself. Google has not productized it; coverage as of mid-2026 still calls it a research project with unresolved battery cost.

THIRD BLOCKER THE TEAM CANNOT ENGINEER AROUND: VALIDATION
PHRM's headline (MAPE <10% vs ECG across three skin-tone groups, daily RHR within ~5 bpm of a wearable) comes from 192,353 training videos / 162,546 validation videos across ~700 participants under IRB protocol. If the spec quotes those numbers as the app's performance, Apple guideline 1.4.1 applies directly: "Apps must clearly disclose data and methodology to support accuracy claims relating to health measurements, and if the level of accuracy or methodology cannot be validated, we will reject your app." (https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/). Borrowing Google's validation for your own model is not disclosure, it is a rejection risk and an investor-facing misstatement.

WHAT DOES SURVIVE (and why it is not a rescue of this claim)
Camera-based heart rate per se is shippable and legal. Heart rate is deliberately absent from the 1.4.1 banned list (which names x-ray, blood pressure, body temperature, blood glucose, blood oxygen "using only the sensors on the device"). Fingertip contact PPG has shipped for 15 years (Instant Heart Rate, Welltory), and foreground facial rPPG ships today via commercial SDKs (Binah SDK, stated App Store / Play compatible, iOS and Android 10+, HR at ~10s: https://www.binah.ai/sdk/). But all of these are FOREGROUND, USER-PRESENT, SPOT-CHECK measurements. Swapping them in does not deliver what the spec cites PHRM for. It deletes the word "passive."

Net: the ruling stands. RESEARCH-ONLY is the right label for the cited capability; note that PLATFORM-BLOCKED applies co-equally to the background/unlock-triggered capture mechanism, and the spec's use of the citation is additionally a citation-status problem (genuine paper, misrepresented as an available capability). Any of the three alone kills it.
result.workaround:
Ship "Morning Pulse Check": a foreground, user-present, 30-second contact PPG spot check, and stop using the word passive.

1) Primary sensor path - fingertip on rear camera + flash, 30-45s, once daily at a fixed time (on waking, before getting out of bed). Zero external hardware, works on any phone including cheap Android in India, and the SNR of contact PPG is far better than facial rPPG, so a 4-person team can actually hit and self-validate acceptable HR error. Shipping precedent is 15 years old and both stores allow it. Yields resting HR and, with care, an HRV proxy (RMSSD).
2) Optional secondary path - foreground facial rPPG during a moment the user is already looking at the app (symptom logging, daily check-in), via a licensed SDK (Binah, NuraLogix DeepAffex, Vastmindz) or an in-house model. Hard rule: enable HR/respiration only. Do NOT surface blood pressure, SpO2, temperature or glucose from those SDKs - Apple 1.4.1 forbids exactly those from device sensors alone and it would take the whole app down.
3) Reframe the product claim honestly - "a 30-second daily resting-HR and HRV trend you take yourself," not "continuous passive monitoring." For an n-of-1 PMOS engine this is arguably the better input anyway: one measurement at a controlled time of day, in a controlled posture, is a cleaner longitudinal series than opportunistic unlock samples that need heavy motion/lighting filtering. Frame it as a 30-second habit tied to an existing ritual, which is the friction level users actually accept - the same tradeoff Welltory and Instant Heart Rate ship on today.
4) Fix the citation in the spec - keep the Nature reference, but move it from "our approach" to a "directional evidence" or "future work" box with an explicit line: "Google's PHRM is a research system; the model and dataset are released under a non-commercial, IRB-gated license, background camera capture is unavailable to third-party apps on both iOS and Android, and no third-party SDK exists. We do not depend on it." Never quote PHRM's MAPE or wearable-parity figures as the app's own accuracy - publish your own bench numbers against a reference or publish none.
5) Only if honest about the grey zone - accept Apple HealthKit / Android Health Connect import of HR data a user's already-owned watch happens to write. Flag it in the spec as an optional enrichment that must never be a prerequisite for any feature, and make every core flow fully functional with zero imported data.
